item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — In his long-awaited return to the Red Sox lineup, Roman Anthony has offered two very different glimpses.
In his first five games, he launched line-to-line rockets while going 10 for 22, five of those hits for extra bases, with a .455/.500/.909 slash line.
Over the next 11 games — including Wednesday’s 7-3 loss at the Rangers when he went 0 for 3 with a walk and a strikeout — he’s hit .149/.216/.213 with 18 strikeouts in 51 plate appearances (35 percent strikeout rate).
So how does the 22-year-old view his performance?
“I’m right where I want to be,” said Anthony.
While Anthony is unhappy with the strikeouts, his swing decisions — attacking strikes, limiting chases — have been close to his norms. He’s swung and missed more than usual (particularly when chasing pitches), but sees that as correctable.
More significantly, as much as Anthony wants to produce, he also appreciates the full arc of his return.
He is checking boxes — the reassurance that he can go on a tear to spearhead the Sox lineup, the need to find his way out of a slump — to regain a normal rhythm in time for the most important stage of the season.
“I came back with enough time to get a good number of plate appearances, and to fail like I am right now and to succeed like I did in the beginning, and then kind of meet in the middle and continue to grind out every single day and get ready for what we want to be a long postseason run,” he said. “[The playoffs are] what you play for after such a long year. … At the end of the day, those few weeks are the only thing that really matters.”
For Anthony, the prospect of the playoffs looms as the ultimate carrot in a tumultuous year. As a rookie in 2025, he offered a dazzling display of talent in the regular season but was reduced to the role of spectating from Fort Myers while rehabbing his oblique strain as the Sox were knocked out of the playoffs by the Yankees in the Wild Card series.
This year, he concluded a stint of nearly four months on the IL due to a partially torn ligament at the base of his right ring finger just in time to get out of Fort Myers and join the Sox in the late stages of their push towards — and, he hopes, deep into — October.
“When you’re part of a team and watching from a distance, it sucks,” said Anthony. “I looked back at last year a lot in the offseason and was like, ‘Man, I wish I was there,’ and just thought of the different scenarios of what could have potentially happened if I was there.
“[That experience] just kind of motivated me to get back there,” he added. “Obviously this year has been a roller coaster. Getting back now and being healthy right now is about getting back there and making sure that I can get that opportunity [to play in the playoffs] this time around.”
For Anthony, the idea of taking part in the playoffs comes with an exciting element of the unknown. And yet he also appreciates that, despite missing last year’s postseason, he has had an experience to prime him for games of immense consequence.
This past March, Anthony experienced the electricity of the World Baseball Classic. He was a game-changer, hitting .280/.400/.520 with two homers and seven RBIs in seven games — a run that included a go-ahead homer to propel Team USA past the Dominican Republic in the semifinals.
Yet that experience, too, left a bit of a bitter aftertaste. In the WBC Final against Venezuela, Anthony struck out for the last out of a 3-2 loss in the championship game.
“[It] went from 100 to zero because I felt like I had done so well and contributed so well … to then, as a person who is hard on himself, being like, ‘Oh man, I should have put the ball in play. I should have done something there,’ ” he reflected.
“That one stung for a little while and took me a little while to kind of work through. You ask any competitor, anytime something ends other than in a win or holding that trophy up, it’s a failure.
“It was a great experience for me. Obviously, that was a sore way to go out. But I learned what that felt like and let it sit with me for a little bit. I was able to work through it and learn [how to handle it] at a young age,” he said. “I haven’t really experienced the other end of that feeling yet.”
Anthony is now chasing that feeling — celebrating with his teammates and pursuing a championship.
“I would much rather be here than being in Fort Myers and watching baseball,” he said. “I’ve learned in my second year now to not look too far ahead and just do everything I can to help the team win today.
“Just taking the field with these guys and getting to play with them every single day is a blast. It’s been great, and we’re to a point now in the year where you’re kind of right where you want to be as a squad.”
Alex Speier can be reached at alex.speier@globe.com. Follow him @alexspeier.

item.title: [heavy.com] Red Sox RP Erik Miller Shares Honest Thoughts on Recent Struggles
item.dc:creator: Dan Morrison
item.description: When the Boston Red Sox sent former top-prospect Marcelo Mayer to the San Francisco Giants for Erik Miller, CBO Craig Breslow was sending a major signal. This season is about winning, and Miller will be more help with that now. For a while, the hard-throwing lefty has been exactly that. A major spark out of the bullpen who makes the Red Sox incredibly intimidating on the mound in the late innings. In his first 14 appearances with Boston, Miller gave up just two runs. The last two games have been
item.content:encoded:
When the Boston Red Sox sent former top-prospect Marcelo Mayer to the San Francisco Giants for Erik Miller, CBO Craig Breslow was sending a major signal. This season is about winning, and Miller will be more help with that now.
For a while, the hard-throwing lefty has been exactly that. A major spark out of the bullpen who makes the Red Sox incredibly intimidating on the mound in the late innings. In his first 14 appearances with Boston, Miller gave up just two runs.
The last two games have been more of a struggle for Miller, though. In 1.1 innings, he’s given up four runs. That includes three runs in Wednesday’s rough loss to the Texas Rangers, which was good enough for Miller to earn a loss.
Boston Red Sox RP Erik Miller Opened Up on Struggles
Following Wednesday’s loss, Erik Miller faced the media following the game. There, he explained that his main issue on Wednesday was that he had control issues. Those control issues put him in bad counts, which made him predictable.
“Just not doing what I’ve been doing well,” Erik Miller said. “Just not getting ahead of guys. Getting behind. Falling into hitters’ counts… Guy knows what’s coming, it usually doesn’t end well. Just kind of working through some stuff right now.”
Red Sox fans and media both noticed Miller saying that he’s working through some stuff. Luckily, that doesn’t mean an injury. It’s more a reference to letting his mechanics get away from him.
“Yeah. Some stuff I’m trying to clean up a little. At some point throughout the year, stuff crops up. You’ve been doing really well and some bad habits kind of come up. So, I’ve just got to work through it. Get back to what I was doing and go from there,” Miller said.
The Red Sox need the version of Miller they’ve largely gotten since the trade. He has a 2.87 ERA in Boston, to go along with a 1.277 WHIP and 14.9 strikeouts per nine. That’s in 15.2 innings over 16 appearances.
Garrett Crochet Will Return to the Red Sox as a Reliever
The Red Sox bullpen is set to get a major boost soon. Ace pitcher Garrett Crochet is getting ready to make his return, but it won’t be as a starter. It’ll be as another power lefty for the bullpen to use.
The expectation had been that Crochet won’t be able to make a rehab and would jump back in right as the first-round of the playoffs start. That may not be the case now. It was recently reported that he could be ready even sooner. That means he’ll potentially pitch in the regular season as a kind of rehab.
“The comebacks of potential October contributors like Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, Johan Oviedo and others might also be aided by the fact the Red Sox might have a week (or more) to set up for the postseason,” Chris Cotillo of MassLive wrote. “It’s not out of the question that the club has someone like Crochet pitch in one of the final regular season games of the year in what’s effectively a rehab outing at the major league level in a game that matters little in the standings.”
It’s excellent news for the Red Sox. With Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, a healthy Garrett Crochet, and Erik Miller, Boston can feel very confident if they get just five innings from a starter.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Milwaukee Brewers: MLB analyst admits he was wrong about Jacob Misiorowski after 2026 Cy-Young worthy season
item.dc:creator: Robin M Adams

They have already clinched their fourth-consecutive National League Central Division crown and are still playing for the top seed in the playoffs. item.content:encoded:
With 10 games left to play in the 2026 MLB regular season, the Milwaukee Brewers are 95-57 and, once again, have the best record in baseball. They have already clinched their fourth-consecutive National League Central Division crown and are still playing for the top seed in the playoffs.
Indeed, a great deal went right for Milwaukee this year, not the least of which being the emergence of Jacob Misiorowski has arguably the best pitcher in the game. After stumbling down the stretch and getting moved to the bullpen in 2025, Misiorowski now is poised to be the Brewers' Game One starter in each postsesaon series that they play.
MLB analyst admits he was wrong about Milwaukee Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski
Milwaukee selected the lanky Misiorowski in the second round of the 2022 MLB Draft. Four years later, he is their ace and a two-time NL All-Star.
There were not many who thought that the 2026 NL Cy Young favorite would be a successful Major League pitcher, though. One of them was Keith Law of The Athletic, who felt that Misiorowski was going to have control issues his whole professional career and/or blow out his arm.
On Thursday morning, he published an article about current Major League players that he was wrong about as prospects. The first one he discusses was Misiorowski.
He wrote, in part:
"I know I wasn't alone in my belief that Misiorowski wouldn't hold up as a starter, either because he wouldn't throw enough strikes or because he would break down. No one has ever thrown this hard, this much, without getting hurt.
"The delivery was still quite rough, and even with the benefit of some of the best stuff in the minors, he still walked almost 15 percent of batters during his time in Double A in 2023 and 2024. He was so inefficient that he'd hit his pitch limits before getting through five innings in the majority of his outings.
"I thought any team would try to smooth out Miz's delivery, but that either it would cost him velocity — that the power was the result of the violence, not held back by it, because who thinks a guy throwing 100 could actually be throwing harder if he had better mechanics? — or that it wouldn't improve his control enough to keep him a starter. Obviously, that didn't end up being the case. His delivery and command improved and he maintained his elite velocity."
Law credits both Misiorowski's desire to improve and the Brewers' organizational coaches for identifying ways to help him improve his command and stay healthy while throwing harder than any starting pitcher in the pitch-tracking era.
The work that Milwaukee has done sure has paid off. With 1-2 starts left in the season, the Brewers ace is 15-5 with a Major League-best 1.89 ERA, 243 strikeouts, and .081 WHIP.
If he is able to maintain the dominance he was shown all year long, and keep opposing hitters from making consistent contact in his final start(s), Misiorowski will set yet another Major League record. Currently, opposing batters are hitting .160 off of him, which is the lowest mark for a starter in baseball history.
Misiorowski proved his doubters wrong. Now, Milwaukee as a team hopes they can do the same by making it to the World Series for the first time since 1982, and winning it for the first time ever.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] The case against Garrett Whitlock returning to Red Sox starting rotation in 2027
item.dc:creator: Katie Manganelli

item.content:encoded:
For the last two seasons, Garrett Whitlock has been one of the best pitchers the Boston Red Sox's bullpen has to offer. But the righty has considered changing that.
Whitlock told Tim Healey of The Boston Globe that he would consider a return to life as a starting pitcher (subscription required). Whitlock in 2021 debuted with Boston as a reliever, but he began starting some games shortly after in 2022. He made four starts in 2024 and planned to take his full season as a starter, but a UCL injury derailed that plan.
“I definitely know my body better and know everything better now, and so it’s definitely something I’d be open to," Whitlock said, via Healey. "So it’s one of those things where the team would have to be on board with it and just talk through everything and go through it. But it’s something I’d always be open to.”
Some fans and people in the Red Sox organization could be excited to hear Whitlock say he's interested in reprising his role as a starting pitcher. Boston has just one righty starter in its rotation this year, Sonny Gray, and he'll be a free agent at the end of the season, barring an unexpected contract extension. Whitlock's success in the bullpen could translate to more in the rotation and he could compete for Gray's former spot.
Red Sox should keep Garrett Whitlock in bullpen despite his willingness to return to a starting role
But Whitlock's history as a starter isn't as clean as it is from the bullpen. Whitlock went on the injured list twice in the 2022-23 seasons with hip and elbow issues. He missed all but four appearances of the 2024 season after he underwent the internal brace procedure to repair his UCL. His elbow even flared up after a period of heavy use out of the bullpen this season. Adding starts into his repertoire hasn't worked before, and though it could work now since Whitlock said he's more in-tune with his body, it isn't a risk the Sox should be willing to take.
Whitlock has had more success as a reliever than as a starter, though he's pitched far more in relief and the sample sizes are far from equal. The veteran has posted a 4.29 ERA over 109 innings across 23 appearances as a starter and a 2.37 ERA over 254.1 frames in relief. The Red Sox need right-handed rotation depth, but they also have Tanner Houck, Kutter Crawford and Johan Oviedo recovering from injury, and none of them have established themselves in another role as seamlessly as Whitlock has.
Whitock told Healey that he would return to a starting role if the Red Sox want him to (he's under team control until after the 2028 season due to two club options) or if any new team he signs with wants him to change. For now and in 2027, the Red Sox should stick with the good thing they have, which is Whitlock as one of the most dangerous relievers in the league.

item.title: [Talk Sox] Roman Anthony Is Agonizingly Close To Breaking Out of His Slump
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: Red Sox Video Roman Anthony couldn't put a ring on it. For more than two months, what had to have been one of the most annoying and nagging injuries kept Anthony out of the Boston Red Sox lineup. He had partially torn a ligament in his right ring finger. It wasn't some massive, noticeable, life-changing injury. It was just an ailment that made it really hard to swing a bat. The Red Sox handled business in the meantime. They went on that franchise record-tying 15-game winning streak. They watched
item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Video
Roman Anthony couldn't put a ring on it. For more than two months, what had to have been one of the most annoying and nagging injuries kept Anthony out of the Boston Red Sox lineup. He had partially torn a ligament in his right ring finger. It wasn't some massive, noticeable, life-changing injury. It was just an ailment that made it really hard to swing a bat.
The Red Sox handled business in the meantime. They went on that franchise record-tying 15-game winning streak. They watched Ceddanne Rafaela become an All-Star. They saw Mickey Gasper temporarily turn into Ted Williams.
Then, in late August, Anthony came back. He was supposed to be the final piece to the puzzle. If the Red Sox were a good baseball team without Anthony, they could potentially be a great one with him -- at least, that's how the thinking went. The problem, though, is clear: Since Anthony has been back, he hasn't been quite right. He hasn't looked like a rising star. He's looked like a hitter who is recognizing that hitting is actually really, really hard.
There's not a whole lot of time for Anthony to right the ship before the postseason, but there's just enough time for Boston fans to hold out hope that he has (or will find) a solution.
If he's going to make fixes, it'll have to be in his approach at the plate, where he's whiffed at a 35% rate in September, including a stretch of 17 strikeouts in 35 plate appearances. Something clearly isn't quite right here, although it may not be as bad as you think.
Roman Anthony's Swing Looks Different When It Matters
One quick way to figure out what might be happening with a hitter who is striking out a lot is to fast forward directly to two-strike counts and see what's happening.
First, though, take a look at what Anthony looks like on the first pitch of an at-bat with two runners on base. This clip shows a wide stance that's slightly open, a strong leg kick, and Anthony's signature ability to stay through the baseball and drive it the other way:

Roman Anthony Since Returning From IL

AB: 61
R: 8
H: 16
HR: 3
RBI: 5
BB: 5
SO: 20
AVG: .262
OPS: .793 pic.twitter.com/zCDEPxL2xi

That's not the swing that Anthony has had lately on two strikes. If you want to be a sad Red Sox fan for a few minutes, this next video is for you (it shows Anthony's recent strikeout stretch). And if you watch closely, you'll see that not only is Anthony not setting up the same each time as on the hit in the video above. He's not even set up the same in all of these clips. Clearly, he's searching for a two-strike solution, but it's changing the openness of his stance, the height at which he stands, the level of his leg kick and even the apparent length of his swing:

Roman Anthony has struck out in 17 of his last 35 plate appearances, and his 2-strike approach has looked completely discombobulated. pic.twitter.com/r3q3tc5A64
— Stats (@redsoxstats) September 12, 2026
Some hitters change their approach with two strikes -- contact hitters in particular often get lower and choke up on the bat to have the best chance of putting the ball in play. But the big and strong Anthony, if he's going to do that, better at least stick to a plan. And it seems like right now he doesn't have one.
So we can see the video, and we can see the basic stats, but to further figure out what's been going wrong with Anthony, we decided to take a look at the metrics behind his swing itself.
Clearly, coming back from a finger injury and a long layoff could make hitting harder, but this isn't just about Anthony's .226 average and .677 OPS in September. The Red Sox need to figure out what's going on so they can address it and improve those numbers the rest of the way.
Lucky for us, Statcast has just about every metric you could possibly imagine, so it's possible to compare all sorts of things about Anthony's swing inputs and batted ball outputs from each month of his rookie season through right now.
Take, for example, his attack angle. That's the vertical direction the sweet spot is traveling when it hits the baseball. This month, Anthony has an attack angle of 16 degrees. When he had a .946 OPS in July of last year, it was 14 degrees. The only time it has ever been this high before was last September in a super small sample size (26 pitches seen). And while it may seem like a minor difference, it can prevent the ideal line drive from coming off Anthony's bat.
That's just one metric. The rest of his bat statistics actually seem fine. Nothing is weird about his bat speed or his swing length or his attack direction. There's nothing underlying there to be totally concerned about.
This is the part, Red Sox fans, where the news gets good.
Roman Anthony Is Actually Just Fine
Anthony's swing, while maybe a little tilted from its optimal self, doesn't seem broken. He's just whiffing a bit more than you'd want. It's also worth considering what happens when Anthony doesn't whiff.
When he's made contact the ball in September, Anthony has hit it harder than ever before. His previous best average exit velocity in a month was in July 2025, at 96.9 miles per hour.
Entering this week, Anthony has averaged 97.0 miles per hour of exit velocity on his batted balls in this month. He's had a hard-hit percentage of 63.6%, right about his career average, and he has the third-best single-month barrel rate of his career. The Red Sox obviously can't afford for him to keep whiffing on more than a third of the swings he takes, but we can also recognize that Anthony is oh so close to putting it back together again.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox Injury Update: SP Garrett Crochet Gets Positive Timeline for Return
item.dc:creator: Dan Morrison
item.description: The regular season is rapidly coming to an end, and the Boston Red Sox still don't have ace pitcher Garrett Crochet back. That could be changing soon, though. It had previously been reported that Crochet was set to return for the first round of the playoffs. Now, Chris Cotillo of MassLive noted in a report that the Red Sox may be pushing to have Crochet pitch in the regular season. This would act as a kind of rehab outing. item.content:encoded:
The regular season is rapidly coming to an end, and the Boston Red Sox still don't have ace pitcher Garrett Crochet back. That could be changing soon, though.
It had previously been reported that Crochet was set to return for the first round of the playoffs. Now, Chris Cotillo of MassLive noted in a report that the Red Sox may be pushing to have Crochet pitch in the regular season. This would act as a kind of rehab outing.
"The comebacks of potential October contributors like Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, Johan Oviedo and others might also be aided by the fact the Red Sox might have a week (or more) to set up for the postseason," Cotillo wrote. "It's not out of the question that the club has someone like Crochet pitch in one of the final regular season games of the year in what's effectively a rehab outing at the major league level in a game that matters little in the standings."
After finishing second in AL Cy Young voting in 2025, 2026 has been a major disappointment for Crochet. He has a 6.30 ERA and hasn't pitched since April 29th, when he originally hit the IL with left shoulder inflammation. He would later also be diagnosed with a lat strain.
When Crochet does return, it won't be in the rotation. He doesn't have time to build up to that. Instead, the Red Sox are going to be using him out of the bullpen. he
Boston Red Sox Ace Garrett Crochet Doesn't Have Time for a Rehab
The reality for Garrett Crochet is that time is running out for a rehab assignment, and he likely won't have time to make one. That's why the Red Sox would likely want to bring him back before a playoff series.
Regardless of if that chance to come back before the postseason happens, however, Crochet is confident in himself.
"Someone brought it up the other day. They were like, isn't that crazy? I'm like, not really," Crochet said on Monday. "I mean, not [to be all] me, me, me, me, but I've done crazy things before. I'm not Joe Schmoe. I've done impressive things. I think that that would be a big ask for some people, but I don't think it's a crazy ask for me."
This isn't entirely new territory for Crochet. In 2020, the Chicago White Sox added him to their postseason roster when he had limited time in live action due to the pandemic and coming out of college. He pitched well in that brief opportunity, throwing 0.2 innings with 2 strikeouts.
The Red Sox Postseason Rotation is Up for Debate
Heading into the postseason, pitching is a strength for the Red Sox. Even with injuries, that much has become obvious. Still, questions remain about the actual rotation in the postseason.
Sonny Gray and Payton Tolle will make starts in a three-game series. That's not up for debate. There is debate about which of the two gets Game One. Then, Game Three is going to be between Ranger Suarez and Jake Bennett. The lean there is certainly for the well-paid Suarez, who is a veteran with postseason success. However, stranger things have happened.
Starters who could be coming back from injury, including Houck and Crochet, are going to be seen as relievers. That's presumably how the Red Sox will also continue to use Brayan Bello and Patrick Sandoval.
Like HEAVY's content? Be sure to follow us.

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — Cody Bradford will start Thursday night for the Texas Rangers in the finale of their three-game series against the Boston Red Sox at Globe Life Field. First pitch is 7:05 p.m. CT on Rangers Sports Network.
Boston has right-hander Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.76 ERA) scheduled. Texas had not named its Thursday starter as of Tuesday.
The Rangers have won the first two games of the series, 4-2 on Tuesday and 7-3 on Wednesday. At 76-76, Texas is tied with the Houston Astros for first place in the American League West. Houston holds the tiebreaker.
Cody Bradford Is 0-5 Since Returning From Elbow Surgery
Bradford (0-5, 4.72 ERA) has made seven starts since the Rangers reinstated him from the 60-day injured list Aug. 5. He had an internal brace procedure on his left elbow in June 2025 and missed that entire season.
Through 34 1/3 innings this year, he has allowed 45 hits and 18 earned runs. He has walked 9 and struck out 17.
His most recent start came Sept. 9 at T-Mobile Park. Bradford allowed 3 runs on 4 hits over 4 innings against the Seattle Mariners, with 2 walks and 1 strikeout. Seattle won 3-2, and MLB.com reported it was Bradford’s fourth straight losing decision, a career high.
A week before that, on Sept. 2 against the Athletics at Globe Life Field, Bradford gave up 3 home runs over 4 innings in a 9-2 loss. Falling behind in counts put him in trouble that afternoon.
“I think fastball command and changeup command were kind of hit and miss today at times,” Bradford said after that start. “I think the inconsistency, falling behind in counts, putting them in hitters’ counts … they made some good damage swings.”
Bradford has not won a major league game since Sept. 18, 2024. That night at Globe Life Field, he held the Toronto Blue Jays scoreless over 7 innings in a 2-0 Rangers win. He finished 2024 with a 3.54 ERA and a 1.01 WHIP over 13 starts.
The Aledo native was a rookie on the Rangers’ 2023 World Series team. Texas drafted him in the sixth round in 2019 out of Baylor.
Sonny Gray Goes for His 18th Win
Gray has a 1.17 WHIP over 156 2/3 innings. The 36-year-old is a three-time All-Star.
On Sept. 11 against the Kansas City Royals at Fenway Park, Gray allowed 3 runs over 6 innings in a 3-2 loss. In his previous start on Sept. 5, he allowed no earned runs over 7 innings against the Baltimore Orioles for his 17th win.
Boston acquired Gray from the St. Louis Cardinals before the season. He is in the final year of a three-year, $75 million contract that includes a mutual option for 2027.
The Red Sox (82-70) have lost five of their last seven games. They hold the second American League wild card, five games ahead of the Chicago White Sox.
The teams met June 12 to 14 at Fenway Park, where Boston won two of three. Texas leads the season series 3-2.
The Rangers are 42-32 at Globe Life Field this season. Toronto visits from Sept. 18 to 20.

item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras exhibió una vez más su poder con el madero al conectar su cuadrangular número 27 de la temporada 2026. En el primer episodio del compromiso ante los Rangers de Texas, el venezolano despachó un elevado entre los jardines izquierdo y central, remolcando al también criollo Wilyer Abreu.
Con este batazo de cuatro esquinas, el criollo cerró la jornada de 3-1 con dos carreras impulsadas, una anotada. Esta actuación le permite continuar firmando una de las campañas más productivas de su carrera profesional, consolidándose como bujía ofensiva de Boston al fijar una nueva marca personal de cuadrangulares en un mismo curso dentro de las Grandes Ligas.
A pesar de la ventaja inicial otorgada por el estacazo de Contreras, la ofensiva de los Medias Rojas se vio silenciada el resto del encuentro al conectar apenas tres imparables en total. Texas reaccionó de manera progresiva y emboscó al relevo visitante en el tramo final con un rally de tres anotaciones en el séptimo inning, dándole la vuelta al marcador para terminar imponiéndose con pizarra de 7-3.
Leer también: Pete Alonso la vuelve a botar en Citi Field y guía la barrida de los Orioles
La derrota recayó sobre el relevista Eric Miller (4-1), mientras que el abridor Nathan Eovaldi (11-9) se acreditó el triunfo por los texanos. Con este resultado, los Medias Rojas de Boston dejan su récord de la temporada en 82-70, ubicándose en la tercera casilla de la División Este de la Liga Americana en plena recta final de la fase regular.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Red Sox held to three hits, drop series to Rangers with lifeless loss

item.content:encoded:
The limp to October goes on for the Boston Red Sox, who blew an early 2-0 lead Wednesday night, and dropped the series in Texas with a 7-3 loss that improved the Rangers to 76-76.
Boston batters managed just three hits, their runs coming via Willson Contreras’ first-inning two-run homer and Caleb Durbin scoring on a balk in the fifth.
Early on, it looked like both starting pitchers were not going to last long.
Rangers lefty MacKenzie Gore began Wednesday’s game with a four-pitch walk, three of which were nowhere near the zone, to Red Sox leadoff man Roman Anthony, and gave up Contreras’ team-leading 27th homer.
Sox rookie southpaw Jake Bennett labored through a 26-pitch bottom of the first in which he faced six batters and gave up a run.
But after a second-inning delay in which it seemed like Gore was about to depart, he completed four innings. Bennett went 4 2/3. Both starters allowed three earned runs, though Gore only yielded two hits to Bennett’s eight.
“Overall, not horrible,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters of Bennett. “The first inning they were able to make him throw some pitches, so the pitches stacked up on him. But at the end of the day, he left with the lead, was competitive. … Usually you’re accustomed to see him pitching deeper, but they were pesky with their at-bats, fouled a lot of stuff off, and drove the count up.”
The Red Sox retook the lead on Jakob Junis’ fifth-inning balk. It evaporated for good one pitch into Greg Weissert’s appearance when he took over for Bennett in the bottom of the inning.
Erik Miller’s three-run blowup seventh inning was the unnecessary coup de grâce for a Red Sox team struggling to so much as collect a hit, much less score a run. But it marked Miller’s worst outing of the season, with Boston or San Francisco, and his third time allowing runs in his last six appearances.
“Just not doing what I’ve been doing well, just not getting ahead of guys, falling behind counts, getting into hitters counts,” a subdued Miller told reporters postgame. “I mean, doesn’t really matter how good your stuff is; guy knows what’s coming, it usually doesn’t end as well.”
“Just kind of working through some stuff right now,” Miller continued. “There’s some stuff (I’m) trying to clean up a little bit on the mechanical side. … At some point throughout the year, stuff crops up. And I’d been doing really well, and some bad habits kind of fallen back into. So yeah, just got to work through it, kind of get back to what I was doing, and go from there.”
2018 World Series hero Nathan Eovaldi closed out the win with four shutout innings against his former team. It marked the veteran righty’s first relief appearance since 2020: Game 4 of the 2021 ALCS with the Red Sox.
To add insult to the injury of Boston’s decision not to re-sign Eovaldi following the 2022 season, his 46 wins since 2023 are tied for second-most among all American League pitchers in that span.
Trevor Story’s infield single in the fifth and Nick Sogard’s pinch-hit single in the sixth comprised the rest of Boston’s hits. The lineup managed three walks and struck out three times in the contest. They were 0 for 7 with runners in scoring position, and left three men on base.
“Yeah, we’re going through it a little bit,” Tracy said of his lineup. “We didn’t have a ton, we didn’t create a ton of opportunities.”
Game highlights were few and far between for the Red Sox. The short list included the usual elite defense from right fielder Wilyer Abreu, who is all but guaranteed to win his third consecutive Gold Glove Award, and continued displays of ABS expertise by new catcher Adley Rutschman, who went 3 for 3 in challenges.
The Red Sox have lost five of their last seven games since their five-game win streak. They are 7-7 in September, 10-11 in their last 20 games, and 82-70 overall.
Their magic number to clinch a postseason spot is five. But there is little magic lately.

Are they just gonna roll right into the playoffs and say, "You know what, Roman, you're the leadoff guy.

Yeah, I think they are gonna go into the postseason with Roman Anthony leading off.
Whether they should or not, it's gonna depend on a lot of the, the next couple weeks, how he performs in that spot.
It hasn't looked good lately.
The last 10 games he's hitting 159, which, I mean, if you're looking at a guy like Roman Anthony, that is, he's supposed to be hitting, you know, 300, hitting with power.
Like, that's just not the guy you expect at the top of that lineup.
So if it keeps up like this, you're gonna have to have a conversation about what is the best option there.
And given how this season has played out, there really haven't been many great options.
And he also seems, and now I'm kinda diving into the brain of Roman Anthony, which is a It seems like he's trying to jump on first pitches, he's trying to sort of guess right and sort of get right that way.
Yeah.
And I just don't know that in the playoffs, you're a leadoff guy, you kinda need more than that.
And again, the issue is, the reason he went back into that spot, they didn't really have a leadoff guy.
Right.
They've, they've tried, I don't know, 11 different people- Everybody in that role all year.
Maybe Yoshida fit, but he's not a guy that plays every day.
Yeah.

Right.

item.content:encoded:
CHICAGO – Pete Crow-Armstrong has joked in the past that he has not put up the best numbers when the Wrigley Field crowd unites in chanting his initials. That perceived trend has not continued with the new chants that roar through the Friendly Confines these days.
When Crow-Armstrong was in the batter’s box in the seventh inning Wednesday night, the calls of “M-V-P! M-V-P!” were already gathering steam. A few seconds later, as the Cubs’ star center fielder rounded the bases after his second home run of the evening, the repetitive cries had become deafening.
In an 8-4 victory over the Braves, Crow-Armstrong continued his assault on the Cubs’ record book and further padded his case to take home the National League’s Most Valuable Player trophy after this incredible campaign. He had a familiar sidekick in Alex Bregman, who finished a single short of the cycle to also help back a quality start from Shota Imanaga.
With the win, the Cubs maintained their half-game lead over the Phillies for the NL’s top Wild Card spot. That said, Chicago owns the tiebreaker over Philadelphia by winning the season series, taking six of seven games against the Phillies in April.
Crow-Armstrong’s two home runs pushed him past Cubs icon and Hall of Famer Billy Williams for the most homers by a left-handed hitter in team history. Williams launched 42 in 1970. Crow-Armstrong added an RBI triple, giving him 81 extra-base hits on the season. That also topped Williams’ single-season club record in that category (80 in 1970) for a lefty batter.
Per MLB.com’s Sarah Langs, this marked the 10th time in Crow-Armstrong’s career that he has collected at least 10 total bases in a game. That is now three more such games than any other player before turning 25 years old, dating back to at least 1900. Only Williams and Sammy Sosa (12 apiece) have more in a Cubs career.
Crow-Armstrong has also tied Nelson Cruz (six in 2019) for the most games with at least 10 total bases in a single season in MLB history, since at least 1900.
Entering play on Wednesday, Crow-Armstrong (4.0) and Bregman (3.1) ranked first and third in the Majors, respectively, during the second half in WAR, per Fangraphs. They have been arguably the top one-two punch in baseball for the past few months and were at it again in the win over the Braves, who are trying to secure the NL East title.
Bregman got the Cubs’ lineup rolling with an RBI double off JR Ritchie in the first inning. Crow-Armstrong then launched his 43rd homer of the season in the third. Bregman followed suit with a leadoff homer (his 26th blast of the year) in the fourth against Ritchie. In the fifth, both Crow-Armstrong and Bregman delivered run-scoring triples to help Chicago pull away.

item.content:encoded:
PCA fortalece su candidatura al JMV con otra noche de múltiples jonrones ante Bravos
This browser does not support the video element.
CHICAGO -- Pete Crow-Armstrong ha bromeado en el pasado con que no ha tenido sus mejores números cuando el público del Wrigley Field se une para corear sus iniciales. Sin embargo, esa aparente tendencia no se ha mantenido con los nuevos cánticos que retumban estos días en el Friendly Confines.
Cuando Crow-Armstrong estaba en la caja de bateo en el séptimo inning la noche del miércoles, los gritos de “¡J-M-V! ¡J-M-V!” ya comenzaban a tomar fuerza. Unos segundos después, mientras el jardinero central estrella de los Cachorros recorría las bases tras conectar su segundo jonrón de la noche, los cánticos se habían vuelto ensordecedores.
En la victoria por 8-4 sobre los Bravos, Crow-Armstrong continuó dejando su huella en el libro de récords de los Cachorros y reforzó aún más su candidatura para llevarse el premio al Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Nacional tras esta increíble campaña. Contó nuevamente con el respaldo de Alex Bregman, quien se quedó a un sencillo de completar el ciclo y también ayudó a respaldar una apertura de calidad de Shota Imanaga.
Con la victoria, los Cachorros mantuvieron su ventaja de medio juego sobre los Filis por el primer puesto de Comodín de la Liga Nacional. Dicho esto, Chicago tiene a su favor el criterio de desempate sobre Filadelfia tras ganar la serie particular, al imponerse en seis de siete juegos contra los Filis en abril.
Los dos jonrones de Crow-Armstrong le permitieron superar al ícono de los Cachorros y miembro del Salón de la Fama Billy Williams, para imponer la mayor cantidad de cuadrangulares de un bateador zurdo en una temporada en la historia de la franquicia. Williams conectó 42 en 1970. Crow-Armstrong también agregó un triple productor, con lo que llegó a 81 extrabases esta temporada. Esa cifra también superó el récord del club para un bateador zurdo en una campaña, establecido por Williams con 80 en 1970.
Según Sarah Langs de MLB.com, ésta fue la 10ma ocasión en la carrera de Crow-Armstrong en la que acumuló al menos 10 bases totales en un juego. Son tres partidos más de ese tipo que cualquier otro jugador antes de cumplir 25 años, desde al menos 1900. Sólo Williams y el dominicano Sammy Sosa, con 12 cada uno, tienen más encuentros así en la historia de los Cachorros.
This browser does not support the video element.
Crow-Armstrong también igualó al dominicano Nelson Cruz, quien tuvo seis juegos de ese tipo en 2019, con la mayor cantidad de encuentros con al menos 10 bases totales en una misma temporada en la historia de MLB, desde al menos 1900.
Antes de la jornada del miércoles, Crow-Armstrong (4.0) y Bregman (3.1) ocupaban el primer y tercer lugar de las Mayores, respectivamente, en WAR durante la segunda mitad de la temporada, según FanGraphs. Podría decirse que han formado una de las mejores duplas del béisbol en los últimos meses y volvieron a demostrarlo en la victoria sobre los Bravos, que buscan asegurar el título del Este de la Liga Nacional.
Bregman puso en marcha la ofensiva de los Cachorros con un doble productor ante JR Ritchie en el primer inning. Crow-Armstrong conectó luego su 43er jonrón de la temporada en el tercero. Bregman hizo lo propio con un cuadrangular abriendo el cuarto episodio ante Ritchie, su 26to vuelacercas del año. En el quinto, Crow-Armstrong y Bregman dispararon triples productores para ayudar a Chicago a ampliar su ventaja.

item.title: [Diario AS] Revelan el oscuro negocio tras las firmas de jóvenes dominicanos para MLB y el escándalo salpica a David Ortiz
item.dc:creator: Ariel Velázquez
item.description: En casi cualquier parque de Grandes Ligas hay una historia dominicana. Puede estar en el lineup, en el bullpen o esperando su turno en el dugouts. La República Dominicana, una pequeña nación del Caribe con menos de 12 millones de habitantes, se convirtió en una de las mayores fábricas de talento del beisbol mundial. Pedro Martínez, Vladimir Guerrero, Adrián Beltré y David Ortiz son parte de esa historia. También lo son Juan Soto, Fernando Tatis Jr. y Junior Caminero, una generación que mantiene
item.content:encoded:
En casi cualquier parque de Grandes Ligas hay una historia dominicana. Puede estar en el lineup, en el bullpen o esperando su turno en el dugouts. La República Dominicana, una pequeña nación del Caribe con menos de 12 millones de habitantes, se convirtió en una de las mayores fábricas de talento del beisbol mundial.
Pedro Martínez, Vladimir Guerrero, Adrián Beltré y David Ortiz son parte de esa historia. También lo son Juan Soto, Fernando Tatis Jr. y Junior Caminero, una generación que mantiene a la isla como uno de los principales proveedores de peloteros para las Grandes Ligas. El año pasado, 144 jugadores dominicanos aparecieron en el Big Show, alrededor del 10 por ciento de todos los peloteros de la liga, de acuerdo con datos recopilados por ProPublica.
Detrás de cada firma existe una industria que comienza mucho antes de que un adolescente pueda ponerse la gorra de un equipo de Grandes Ligas. Entre 2012 y principios de 2026, las organizaciones de MLB pagaron 1,042 millones de dólares en bonos a prospectos dominicanos, de acuerdo con el análisis de ProPublica. Ese dinero alimenta a entrenadores, academias, intermediarios y prestamistas que conocen el sistema desde mucho antes de que el jugador llegue a un estadio de Grandes Ligas.
¿Cómo las mafias se aprovechan de los prospectos?
El problema comienza incluso antes de que exista una firma oficial. Los llamados preacuerdos permiten que equipos y prospectos pacten cantidades con años de anticipación, pese a que los jugadores internacionales no pueden firmar oficialmente hasta cumplir 16 años. Para las familias, el bono que algún día llegará puede convertirse desde mucho antes en una garantía para conseguir dinero inmediato.
Los entrenadores suelen recibir una parte importante del bono por haber formado al jugador, proporcionarle vivienda, alimentación y entrenamiento. ProPublica encontró casos en los que esa comisión llegó al 35 o 50 por ciento. Después aparecen los prestamistas, que entregan dinero a las familias utilizando como garantía una parte del futuro bono.
Una abogada que ha representado a jóvenes peloteros en disputas con entrenadores y prestamistas estimó que 80% de los bonos de Grandes Ligas pagados a prospectos dominicanos tienen algún préstamo asociado. Se calcula que hasta 500 millones de dólares de los 1,042 millones entregados entre 2012 y 2026 podrían terminar rápidamente en manos de entrenadores y prestamistas.
En ese mundo aparece Santo Caraballo. ProPublica lo describe como uno de los prestamistas más conocidos del beisbol dominicano. Su negocio consistía en entregar dinero a familias cuyos hijos tenían un preacuerdo con una organización de Grandes Ligas y cobrar después cantidades mucho mayores, utilizando el futuro bono como garantía. Caraballo defendió el modelo al explicar que el riesgo también estaba de su lado.
“Tú no sabes si se va a dar o no se va a dar, porque si el pelotero no firma, no cobras”, dijo en una entrevista a ProPublica.
Uno de los casos investigados es el de Belfi Rivera, quien a los 14 años llegó a un acuerdo verbal con los Diamondbacks por 1.8 millones de dólares. Cuando llegó el momento de cobrar, 630,000 dólares fueron para su entrenador, John Carmona, por una comisión equivalente al 35%. Más de 950,000 dólares terminaron en manos de Caraballo.
La familia de Belfi, de acuerdo con ProPublica, recibió inicialmente alrededor de 25,000 dólares. Los padres afirmaron que Caraballo les prestó ese dinero a cambio de recibir una cantidad mucho mayor cuando llegara el bono. La familia tenía poca experiencia financiera y, según el reportaje, ni siquiera recibió una copia del contrato que firmó.
Pero el nombre que hizo todavía más atractiva aquella relación fue el de David Ortiz.
Los padres de Belfi dijeron a ProPublica que Caraballo se presentó como la “mano derecha” de Ortiz. La reputación de Big Papi, una de las figuras más reconocidas de la historia reciente del beisbol dominicano, ayudó a generar confianza en una familia que estaba entrando por primera vez a un mundo en el que se manejaban cientos de miles de dólares.
Después, según los padres, Caraballo les habló de la posibilidad de invertir el dinero que todavía recibirían de los Diamondbacks en un negocio relacionado con él y Ortiz.
“Yo me puse contento porque ya mi muchacho va a tener una gente que le puede dar un consejo”, contó Eduardo Rivera a ProPublica.
La relación entre Ortiz y Caraballo no era una invención. Registros corporativos de Florida muestran que en 2021 ambos estuvieron vinculados con Big Papi Sports Group, una empresa que fue disuelta al año siguiente. Ortiz reconoció ante ProPublica que había invertido millones de dólares en el negocio de beisbol de Caraballo, aunque no precisó cuánto dinero ni identificó la empresa.
Ortiz aseguró que su relación empresarial con Caraballo estaba limitada a préstamos para entrenadores y que no trabajaba directamente con los padres de los prospectos porque recuperar ese dinero resultaba complicado. Sin embargo, ProPublica encontró un documento judicial en el que aparece el nombre de Ortiz en un contrato firmado con los padres de un jugador de 13 años.
El acuerdo establecía que Ortiz y Caraballo proporcionarían al menor alimentación, vivienda, estudios, entrenamiento, ropa, suplementos y oportunidades para ser observado por scouts. A cambio, recibirían 35% de su eventual bono de firma.
El jugador nunca firmó con una organización de Grandes Ligas y la demanda relacionada con el acuerdo fue desechada por cuestiones procesales. El documento, sin embargo, muestra que al menos en un caso el nombre de Ortiz sí apareció directamente en un contrato relacionado con un menor y con el futuro bono de un prospecto.
La investigación también documentó que Caraballo utilizaba la relación con Ortiz como parte de su capital de confianza. Padres, entrenadores y abogados consultados por ProPublica dijeron que el prestamista mencionaba al al Miembro del Salón de la Fama durante sus negocios.
Ortiz, por su parte, rechazó haber autorizado ese uso de su nombre.
“Yo nunca autoricé a Santo Caraballo a usar mi nombre o mi reputación para ganar la confianza de jóvenes peloteros o sus familias, para promover préstamos o inversiones, o para representar transacciones financieras como si fueran personalmente respaldadas por mí”, cito el reportaje por medio de un documento compartido por el abogado de Ortiz.
“Yo nunca participaría a sabiendas en ninguna operación que tenga la intención de tomar ventaja de un joven jugador o su familia”, extendió la cita.
Ortiz dijo además que comenzó a alejarse de Caraballo después de observar conductas que consideró inapropiadas. Según su declaración, la relación empresarial “comenzó a llegar a su fin” hace más de 18 meses y la relación personal terminó aproximadamente entre un año y medio y dos años antes de sus declaraciones a ProPublica.
La investigación, sin embargo, encontró una imagen que complica esa cronología. En septiembre de 2025, Ortiz y Caraballo viajaron juntos en un avión privado rumbo a Puerto Rico para asistir a un concierto de Bad Bunny.
La batalla de Ortiz en la disputa laboral de 2022
En 2022, MLB y el Sindicato de Jugadores negociaban un nuevo contrato colectivo y uno de los puntos más importantes era la posibilidad de establecer un draft internacional. La propuesta habría eliminado los preacuerdos que permiten a equipos y jugadores pactar cantidades antes de la edad oficial para firmar.
MLB defendía el draft como una manera de terminar con ese sistema. El sindicato se oponía porque consideraba que limitaría la capacidad de los prospectos para elegir equipo y eliminaría la competencia entre organizaciones que ayuda a elevar los bonos.
Ortiz intervino públicamente en favor de rechazar el draft. En un mensaje de voz dirigido a jugadores y entrenadores dominicanos, pidió organizar una campaña de oposición.
“Si permitimos que el draft suceda aquí en la República Dominicana, hasta sus tataranietos, y todos los demás, se verán afectados por él”, dijo Ortiz, según el audio obtenido por ProPublica. “Si dejamos que nos impongan eso aquí, estaremos en graves problemas”.
El draft no fue incluido finalmente en el acuerdo entre MLB y el sindicato.
Cuando ProPublica preguntó directamente a Ortiz si su oposición estaba relacionada con sus intereses empresariales junto a Caraballo, el exjugador no respondió y terminó la llamada.
Posteriormente, a través de su abogado, Ortiz negó que existiera una motivación económica detrás de su postura.
“Mi oposición a la propuesta de la liga nunca estuvo motivada por intereses personales”, señaló.
Según el comunicado, su postura estaba basada en sus opiniones sobre el desarrollo de los peloteros dominicanos y en el impacto que, a su juicio, tendría un draft internacional sobre el beisbol en el país.
El reportaje de ProPublica no establece que Ortiz haya cometido personalmente fraude o usura, ni que haya cobrado directamente los préstamos de los jóvenes. Documenta una relación empresarial y personal con Caraballo, un prestamista que obtuvo importantes cantidades de dinero de bonos de prospectos dominicanos.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Pete Crow-Armstrong, Alex Bregman make MLB history with rare feat in Cubs' rout over Braves
item.dc:creator: Ryan Young
item.description: Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman made MLB history on Wednesday night while leading the Chicago Cubs to a blowout win over the Atlanta Braves. Crow-Armstrong and Bregman each had a home run, each had a triple and each had three extra-base hits in the 8-4 rout at Wrigley Field. item.content:encoded:
Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman made MLB history on Wednesday night while leading the Chicago Cubs to a blowout win over the Atlanta Braves.
Crow-Armstrong and Bregman each had a home run, each had a triple and each had three extra-base hits in the 8-4 rout at Wrigley Field. That made them the first pair of MLB teammates to do that in the same game in nearly 70 years.
The last pair of teammates to pull that feat off was Willie Mays and Daryl Spencer for the San Francisco Giants in 1958, according to OptaStats.
Bregman came just short of hitting for the cycle in the win. He hit an RBI double in the opening inning to put the Cubs on the board first, and then got his solo homer in the fourth.
The best shot, though, came in the fifth. Bregman hit a two-RBI triple that just barely made it past Braves third baseman Austin Riley up the line. That put the Cubs up 6-0 at the time.
Crow-Armstrong got his home run first, also a solo shot in the third inning. He hit a second solo home run the seventh, too, and hit an RBI triple in the fifth inning just two batters ahead of Bregman.
The Braves added two runs in the ninth inning, off of a Mauricio Dubon double and an RBI from Sean Murphy, but their comeback started too late. The Cubs held on to grab the four-run win easily.
The Cubs have now won four of their last six games, and sit at 85-68 on the year. The Milwaukee Brewers have already clinched the NL Central, but the Cubs still have a two-game lead in the NL wild-card race.
The loss for the Braves dropped them to 89-64 on the season. They've still got the lead in the NL East, but by just a handful of games over the Philadelphia Phillies. A win for them on Wednesday night, along with some help from elsewhere in the league, could have clinched a postseason spot.
Both teams still have a bit of work to do to ensure a postseason berth. But the Cubs, thanks to Bregman and Crow-Armstrong, seem well on their way.

item.title: [Boston.com] Chad Tracy hints at Red Sox calling up Triple-A player with 60 steals for postseason
item.dc:creator: Conor Ryan
item.description: Chad Tracy and the Red Sox still have plenty of work to do when it comes to clinching a playoff berth in the coming days. After that, it’s about formulating the best postseason roster to overcome a seemingly inevitable best-of-three series in the Bronx. One priority for Boston? With runs at a premium in October, teams
item.content:encoded:
Chad Tracy and the Red Sox still have plenty of work to do when it comes to clinching a playoff berth in the coming days.
After that, it’s about formulating the best postseason roster to overcome a seemingly inevitable best-of-three series in the Bronx.
One priority for Boston? Adding speed to the roster once the calendar flips to the postseason, especially with Eli White likely sidelined for the start of the playoffs due to a ligament injury in his foot.
With runs at a premium in October, teams often tend to put an emphasis on adding players in the playoffs who can swipe a base or two at a crucial time — as evidenced by Dave Roberts in 2004 and Quintin Berry in 2013 with Boston.
As such, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy acknowledged on WEEI’s “Rich and Ken with Ted Johnson” that he might consider calling up Worcester Red Sox outfielder Braiden Ward for the postseason roster — in what would be his first games in the big leagues.
It might be an unorthodox move when it comes to throwing a career minor-leaguer directly into the fire of playoff baseball, but Ward’s skillset is evident.
The 27-year-old Ward has been a monster on the basepaths down in Triple-A — stealing 60 bases in 106 games for the Woo Sox while only getting caught nine times.
Ward has been a sparkplug since arriving in the Red Sox organization as part of a November trade with the Rockies — with the speedster setting a Grapefruit League record during spring training after stealing 19 bases in just 27 games.
Speaking ahead of Boston’s game against the Rangers, Tracy added that Ward is the type of player who could serve a critical role come October.
“It’s just hard to say, other than to say he has stolen 60 bases,” Tracy told MassLive’s Chris Cotillo. “It’s very obvious you have a guy down there that has a really good ability to run and steal bases. We’ll see [when] we get at the end of the season and how all that fits.”
Even though Ward’s bat may not stand out (.243 batting average), the Red Sox would likely only utilize him for late-game situations on the basepaths.
During that 2004 run to a World Series, Roberts appeared in three games for Boston but did not record a single plate appearance.
“Every time he gets on, he’s not afraid,” Tracy added of Ward while speaking to Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. “That’s the thing. He gets on base, he’s looking to go. That’s a unique trait. There’s a lot of guys that can run and steal bases, and then there’s other guys that every single time I get on, almost regardless of the time of the pitcher, I feel like I can outrun the ball.”

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red are losers of four games out of their last six after dropping Tuesday's 4-2 decision to the Texas Rangers.
As they push to clinch a playoff spot, the Red Sox send rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69, 83 K) to the mound in the middle contest of the three game series in Texas.
Just hours before first pitch, the Red Sox announced a decision on their left-swinging outfielder Jarren Duran.
Duran is sitting out again Wednesday as the Boston Red Sox face Texas Rangers left-hander MacKenzie Gore, extending a pattern now seven starts deep. The decision appears to be strictly a platoon move by interim manager Chad Tracy. There have been no reports that Duran is injured.
In fact, Boston has now benched its left-handed-hitting outfielder against every left-handed starter he has faced since Aug. 8, a stretch that raises concerns about how Duran fits into next season's outfield picture, and for the likely American League wild-card series matchup.
In that three-game series, the Red Sox appear certain to face at least one left-hander, possibly two, in Yankees starters Max Fried and Carlos Rodón.

| SP: Jake Bennett (LHP) • 9-7, 3.69 ERA | | | | |
| September 16, 2026 • Globe Life Field, Arlington, TX • 8:05 PM ET • Red Sox at Rangers | | | | |
| # | Player | Pos | AVG | SLG |
| 1 | Roman Anthony | LF | .240 | .371 |
| 2 | Jahmai Jones | DH | .214 | .379 |

| Lineups confirmed. Season stats shown (AVG / SLG). Umpire: Nick Mahrley • Weather: 97°, Wind 9 mph • O/U: 8 Runs • Line: BOS -112 / TEX -108. | | | | |
Jarren Duran's Platoon Pattern Against Lefties
Duran bats left-handed, Gore throws left-handed, and Boston's coaching staff has ceased to start Duran on days a southpaw takes the mound for the opponent.
Nate Eaton takes over in center field for Boston.
Texas had already turned in its own lineup behind Gore hours before first pitch, setting up the Wednesday matchup at Globe Life Field.
Duran's absence from the lineup against lefties has stretched to seven straight starts without facing a southpaw, dating back to his last look at left-handed pitching on Aug. 8, according to RotoWire. He sat again Sunday against Kansas City and was used only as a pinch-hitter, a role he has filled repeatedly this month.
There is no reported health issue behind Tracy's decision. Duran started Tuesday against right-hander Jacob deGrom, playing center field and batting seventh, and remains fully active on Boston's roster.
Duran is slashing .204/.261/.361 with 20 home runs across 141 games this season, and his OPS against left-handed pitching sits at .641, actually higher than his .616 mark against right-handers, according to FanGraphs. Boston has kept sitting him against lefties anyway.
| TEXAS RANGERS STARTING LINEUP | | | | |
| SP: MacKenzie Gore (LHP) • 8-11, 4.62 ERA | | | | |
| September 16, 2026 • Globe Life Field, Arlington, TX • 8:05 PM ET • Red Sox at Rangers | | | | |
| # | Player | Pos | AVG | SLG |
| 1 | Justin Foscue | 2B | .268 | .493 |
| 2 | Corey Seager | SS | .234 | .438 |
| 3 | Josh Jung | 3B | .294 | .436 |
| 4 | Jake Burger | 1B | .232 | .424 |
| 5 | Brandon Nimmo | RF | .263 | .413 |
| 6 | Wyatt Langford | LF | .239 | .435 |
| 7 | Ezequiel Duran | CF | .271 | .441 |
| 8 | Elias Díaz | DH | .239 | .405 |
| 9 | Danny Jansen | C | .192 | .359 |
| Lineups confirmed. Season stats shown (AVG / SLG). Umpire: Nick Mahrley • Weather: 97°, Wind 9 mph • O/U: 8 Runs • Line: BOS -112 / TEX -108. | | | | |
Duran's Playing Time Has Dropped Sharply
Duran appeared in 160 games in 2024, when he led the American League in at-bats, doubles and triples, on his way to an All-Star selection and an eighth-place MVP finish. He followed that with 157 games in 2025.
This year he has played in 141 of Boston's games, a drop that traces to the growing run of benchings against left-handed hurlers. Wednesday marks at least the seventh time this season Boston has parked Duran for a left-handed starter, following earlier sit-downs against Rodón, Kyle Freeland, Jacob Lopez, Mitch Bratt and Reid Detmers, according to CBS Sports.
Boston opened the year with four outfielders competing for time, but an early injury to Roman Anthony briefly opened the picture before Duran struggled through a rough first half, batting .194 over his first 87 games. The Duran platoon has held even as the outfield picture has grown thinner. Ceddanne Rafaela remains out with a quad injury and Eli White is sidelined with a foot issue, leaving Eaton as the only regular right-handed option in center on days Duran sits.
With the Red Sox pushing for playoff position down the stretch, Duran's shrinking role against left-handed pitching will keep drawing scrutiny. Entering Wednesday's game, the Red Sox magic number for clinching a playoff berth is five — meaning that any combination of Red Sox wins and Chicago White Sox losses totaling five puts Boston in the postseason.

item.title: [NBC Boston] Projecting the Red Sox' Wild Card Series rotation
item.dc:creator: Justin Leger
item.description: The Boston Red Sox haven't officially clinched a postseason spot, but all signs point toward a Wild Card Series rematch at Yankee Stadium. Pitching depth was a problem for the Red Sox in last year's playoff meeting with the Yankees. Their ace Garrett Crochet propelled them to victory in Game 1, but Brayan Bello and an inexperienced Connelly Early couldn't get the job done in Games 2 and 3. This time, Boston's pitching will be a strength. Veteran right-hander Sonny Gray, rookie southpaw Payton To
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox haven't officially clinched a postseason spot, but all signs point toward a Wild Card Series rematch at Yankee Stadium.
Pitching depth was a problem for the Red Sox in last year's playoff meeting with the Yankees. Their ace Garrett Crochet propelled them to victory in Game 1, but Brayan Bello and an inexperienced Connelly Early couldn't get the job done in Games 2 and 3.
This time, Boston's pitching will be a strength. Veteran right-hander Sonny Gray, rookie southpaw Payton Tolle, and veteran lefty Ranger Suarez can go toe-to-toe with most clubs' 1-through-3. The question is, what's the optimal order to put them in for the three-game Wild Card Series?
It's a good problem to have, and there's really no wrong answer. That said, here's our ideal Wild Card Series rotation for Boston as it looks to avenge last year's crushing defeat:
Justin Leger
Game 1: Sonny Gray
Gray isn't the "sexy" pick. That would be the mustached man I have starting Game 2.
But in what's sure to be an electrifying environment at Yankee Stadium, I want a dependable veteran on the mound to begin the series. I want Mr. Consistency.
All season long, Gray has fit that description.
Gray has a 17-5 record (tied for MLB lead in wins) with a 2.76 ERA through 27 starts. Since Crochet went down with an early-season injury, the 36-year-old has stepped up as the Red Sox' de facto ace with 18 quality starts (tied for seventh in MLB).
Unlike Tolle, Gray has plenty of experience pitching at Yankee Stadium. He's had his fair share of rough starts there throughout his 14-year career, especially during his brief stint with New York, but he was solid there earlier this season with three earned runs across 6.1 innings pitched in a 5-3 victory. In his other start against the Yankees at Fenway Park, he took a no-hitter into the eighth inning.
It'll be an uphill battle for the Red Sox regardless of who's on the mound, because Cy Young frontrunner Cam Schlittler will be poised to shut down Boston's bats yet again. Still, Gray can be counted on to give the Sox a chance to win, and if they lose, they'll have great options to lean on in Games 2 and 3.
Game 2: Payton Tolle
If Tolle is named the Red Sox' Game 1 starter, I won't complain. I'd be slightly concerned that his 0.1 IP in last year's Wild Card Series marks his only experience pitching at Yankee Stadium, but that isn't worth panicking about. He seems built for the bright lights.
Tolle looked sharp in both of his starts against the Yankees at Fenway this season. During his first outing in April, the 23-year-old allowed just one run on three hits across six innings. In his second start against them in June, he carried a perfect game into the sixth inning, finishing with no runs and just one hit allowed over seven innings pitched.
Those were two of many outings this season in which Tolle has looked like an ace. He'll have to perform like one throughout Boston's postseason run, and if he gets the ball in Game 2, he might be counted on to keep Boston's season alive.
Game 3: Ranger Suarez
If it comes down to a do-or-die Game 3, I feel great about Ranger Suarez taking the mound. The 31-year-old veteran has the postseason pedigree with an impressive 1.48 ERA in 11 career appearances (eight starts) with the Philadelphia Phillies.
Suarez endured a second-half slump but has looked more like himself in his last two outings. After tossing seven shutout innings against the Baltimore Orioles on Sept. 4, he allowed just one run across seven innings while striking out eight Kansas City Royals hitters on Saturday. This is the version of Suarez the Red Sox expected to get when they signed him to a five-year, $130 million contract in the offseason.
If Suarez struggles, the Red Sox will have the luxury of an elite bullpen to lean on. Brayan Bello has been an excellent bulk option since reverting to a relief role. Jake Bennett could be a legitimate weapon out of the 'pen as well, along with Crochet if he returns in time from his injury.
Mitchael Hurley
Game 1: Payton Tolle
I'm not opposed to statistics influencing baseball decisions. I rely on statistics more than I should.
But in this case, I don't think they matter. If you've watched the Red Sox this year, it could not be more clear that Payton Tolle is very much the heart and soul of this team. And the idea of sending him out onto the mound at Yankee Stadium with the whole baseball world watching just feels like the obvious choice.
If the Red Sox are going to win a series like this one, they're going to need to be the team with more energy. Nobody would bring more juice to the mound than Tolle. If he can step onto the field on a rainy Sunday four hours after first pitch was scheduled and instantly deliver an immaculate inning in the first, it's frightening to think what type of energy he can bring to a Game 1 start.
The Yankees have struggled against him this year, but even if they hadn't, I've gotta send Tolle to the mound for Game 1.
Game 2: Sonny Gray
In another year, in another circumstance, the 36-year-old Sonny Gray would be in line to win his first career Cy Young Award.
Of course, Cam Schlittler, the Yankees' presumed Game 1 starter, has wrecked any and all Cy Young debate with his sterling season in New York. Still, Gray is having one of the best seasons of his 14-year career, and he has to pitch in this series.
He did allow a pair of homers in his lone start at Yankee Stadium this season, and he's given up 22 homers in 23 appearances there in his career. With the short porch looming and the crowd always looking to erupt, that would be my concern.
But Gray's been great all year, he's been great down the stretch, and the Red Sox will ensure that he's properly rested for this one.
Game 3: Ranger Suarez
Would it look bad if the Red Sox potentially lost the series in two games and never sent Ranger Suarez and his 1.48 postseason ERA to the mound? It sure would.
But given the years that Tolle and Gray have had, I think the Red Sox could live with it.
There is some concern that he got rocked in the Bronx on Aug. 30 (six earned runs in 5.1 innings), but he also allowed one run in six innings in his first start at Yankee Stadium earlier in the season.
Considering the Red Sox had to send rookie Connelly Early out there in Game 3 a year ago to make his fifth career start, the team is clearly in a much better position if another Game 3 awaits them in the Bronx.

item.title: [roundtable.io] Could Spring Training Standout Replace Injured Eli White on Boston Red Sox Playoff Roster?
item.dc:creator: Zach Coe
item.description: Alex Cora said Braiden Ward would be a factor in October. The Boston Red Sox outfield depth took a major hit ahead of last Friday’s series opener against the Kansas City Royals as the team placed Eli White on the 10-day injured list with a right foot ligament injury, with no timetable for his return. item.content:encoded:
Alex Cora said Braiden Ward would be a factor in October.
The Boston Red Sox outfield depth took a major hit ahead of last Friday’s series opener against the Kansas City Royals as the team placed Eli White on the 10-day injured list with a right foot ligament injury, with no timetable for his return. The 32-year-old outfielder not only filled in admirably for the injured Ceddanne Rafaela, but was also slated to play an important role on the postseason roster as the fourth outfielder and pinch runner off the bench. With White now unlikely to return before the postseason, could the Red Sox turn to spring-training standout Braiden Ward to fill the role?
About Ward
The Red Sox acquired Ward in an offseason deal with the Colorado Rockies in exchange for left-handed reliever Brennan Bernardino. The 27-year-old outfielder became one of the biggest storylines of Red Sox spring training, seeing ample playing time as many of Boston's outfield options, including Roman Anthony, Wilyer Abreu and Rafaela, represented their countries in the World Baseball Classic. In 27 Grapefruit League games, Ward hit .378/.509/.444/.953 while stealing 19 bases, setting a single-season spring training record. Ward's dynamic speed caught the eye of now-former manager Alex Cora, who told reporters on several occasions that the 27-year-old would be a factor come October.
After missing the team's opening-day roster amid an already crowded outfield, Ward spent the entire 2026 season in Triple-A Worcester. In 107 games with the WooSox, Ward hit just .238/.356/.355/.711 but set a record for most stolen bases in a single season for a Red Sox Triple-A club with 58 and counting.
There's just one problem...
While Ward seems like a slam-dunk option to fill White's role on the postseason roster, it is not as simple as just recalling him from Triple-A, as he's not on the 40-man roster. The Red Sox 40-man roster currently sits at 39; however, the impending returns of Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo mean the team will have to either designate two players for assignment or move someone to the 60-day IL.
Luckily, there are several candidates for the latter: in White, should he be unable to return for the postseason, designated hitter Masataka Yoshida, utility man Anthony Seigler and reliever Justin Slaten, all of whom appear unlikely to return prior to the end of the season.
Is Ward actually an option?
Interim manager Chad Tracy was asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league club during his weekly appearance on WEEI's 'Rich and Ken with Ted Johnson' Show on Wednesday afternoon. "I think that'd be considered for sure," he said when asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league team. "It's really hard to predict what a roster could look like, but you definitely can't ignore a 60-stolen-base player," he continued.
However, Tracy cautioned that a pinch runner is a last resort for a team when it's trailing, and teams must consider other options, like whether it would be more valuable to add another right-handed bat or a better defender to the roster. Though Ward does profile as an above-average outfield defender.
Up next for the Sox
After falling 4-2 in Tuesday night's series opener, the Red Sox will look to even up the three-game set with the Texas Rangers in game two of three from Globe Life Field on Wednesday night. Rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite fellow southpaw MacKenzie Gore (8-11, 4.62 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

The right-hander entered in the seventh and struck out Oliver Dunn looking at a 94.1 mph fastball. He then walked a batter before getting Austin Slater to swing through a 93.6 mph four-seamer and Jack Suwinski to chase an 83.5 mph sweeper. Houck threw 22 pitches (11
item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON -- Tanner Houck continued his rehab assignment with his third Minor League appearance on Tuesday, while Garrett Crochet threw another bullpen session at Fenway Park as both worked toward returning to Boston in relief roles.
The right-hander entered in the seventh and struck out Oliver Dunn looking at a 94.1 mph fastball. He then walked a batter before getting Austin Slater to swing through a 93.6 mph four-seamer and Jack Suwinski to chase an 83.5 mph sweeper.
Houck threw 22 pitches (11 strikes) and reached 94.2 mph with his fastball.
The 30-year-old is expected to make his next appearance on Friday, when he is scheduled for a longer outing in the 45-, 50-pitch range.
“Obviously some swing and miss in there. He has that capability,” interim manager Chad Tracy said ahead of Boston's bout with the Rangers Wednesday. “We all know -- and he said [it] himself, each time he touches the mound, getting his rhythm -- he gets a little bit more comfortable. That's all part of it. The strike-throwing piece and getting command of your pitches.
“So it seems at this point he's at least taking a step forward each time he goes out there, which is good. This next one will be good, being able to see [if he can] replicate that over a longer stretch of pitches.”
Crochet also took another step in his recovery.
The 2025 American League Cy Young Award runner-up threw a 30-pitch bullpen session at Fenway Park. Tracy said the session went well, but as of Wednesday the team did not have much clarity on Crochet’s next steps. He will continue his throwing program this week before the Red Sox re-evaluate him over the weekend.
Crochet has been building up his workload and intensity in recent bullpen sessions. He threw 25 pitches in his previous session Friday, when he incorporated his sweeper and threw his fastball in the 92-93 mph range.

item.content:encoded:
Since returning from injury on August 30, Roman Anthony has looked more like the 2025 version of himself than he did at the beginning of the season. He's hitting .258 with a .764 OPS. In his 15 games, he's got five RBI and six extra-base hits; it's good for a 109 WRC+. It's exactly what the Red Sox needed from him in his return from his May 4 injury.
The one thing Anthony has struggled with has been leading off the game. He has hit leadoff in every game he's played since his return and has only two singles, a double, and five strikeouts with no walks in that spot. It's probably time to have someone else lead off.
In his absence (May 5-August 29), Red Sox leadoff hitters had success in the first inning. While they only hit .213, they had a .307 on-base percentage and a .449 slugging percentage, which equated to a 108 WRC+. Surprisingly, most of that success came from Jarren Duran, who hit leadoff 31 of the 101 games and had a 141 WRC+.
Roman Anthony hasn't performed in the first inning, but he has the rest of the game
Anthony has struggled in the leadoff spot all season. In a total of 36 games, the lefty has a .299 OPS in the first inning. In the second inning or later this season, Anthony boasts a .280/.395/.439/.834 slash line and a 136 WRC+. In those same innings, in only the games he was first in the batting order, he has a .792 OPS and 125 WRC+.
Something about him batting first in the first inning isn't working for him. Whether it's his approach or the way pitchers are attacking him in that spot, Anthony hasn't been able to put it together this season. That's why it's time to drop him down in the order.
That doesn't mean to all of a sudden move him down to seventh in the order, but to push him down to second or third and put a player with high on-base skills in front of him. The Sox have had a few players show really great on-base skills this season. Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, and Isiah Kiner-Falefa are all players with an OBP over .340 this season. Having one of them leadoff, then getting on base in front of Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela, Willson Contreras, and Wilyer Abreu would be extremely dangerous.
Anthony hasn't shown he can hack it leading off the game this season; it's been his one real weak point since his return. With two weeks until the start of the playoffs and a postseason berth almost assured (100% per FanGraphs as of September 15th), now is the time to experiment with the lineup and fix this problem before they get to October.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox fell to the Texas Rangers on Tuesday night in their series opener, 4-2.
Now, ahead of Wednesday’s game, which will feature left-handed pitchers Jake Bennett for Boston and MacKenzie Gore for the Rangers, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy made some sudden changes to his starting lineup, one of which includes fan favorite slugger Mickey Gasper.
Red Sox Make Sudden Gasper Decision
At times this season, Gasper has been a major spark in the Red Sox lineup. And although he’s gone up and down from Triple-A to the majors, the Red Sox have kept him on the big league roster since recalling him Aug. 31 after Willson Contreras suffered an injury.
However, after logging two at-bats as a starter on Tuesday, recording one hit before Jahmai Jones replaced him as the designated hitter, Gasper will get the day off on Wednesday.
Jones is slotted to start as the DH and will bat in the two-hole, with Gasper available off the bench if needed.
Here’s Boston’s lineup:
Via Underdog MLB: “Red Sox 9/16 R. Anthony LF J. Jones DH W. Abreu RF W. Contreras 1B A. Rutschman C C. Durbin 3B T. Story SS I. Kiner-Falefa 2B N. Eaton CF J. Bennett SP.”

W. Contreras 1B
A. Rutschman C

T. Story SS

J. Bennett SP
— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) September 16, 2026
Gasper’s 2026 Season
Gasper, 30, made his MLB debut with the Red Sox back in 2024. After spending 2025 with the Minnesota Twins, he returned to Boston this offseason and has managed to carve out a role.
He has played in 58 games this season and owns a .267 batting average, 25 runs, 46 hits, nine home runs, and 23 RBIs, while posting a .488 slugging percentage and an .866 OPS.
