item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Sit Jarren Duran, Shake Up Lineup For Rangers Matchup originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Boston Red Sox will give their lineup a significantly different look Wednesday night as they attempt to respond to a frustrating series-opening loss. Jarren Duran is out of the starting lineup against Texas Rangers left-hander MacKenzie Gore. Mickey Gasper and Nick Sogard also will begin the game on the bench after starting Tuesday's 4-2 defeat at Globe Life Field.
Jahmai Jones will replace Gasper at designated hitter and bat second. Isiah Kiner-Falefa enters at second base, while Nate Eaton will take over for Duran in center field.
Boston officially announced its revamped batting order on X before the second game of the three-game series. Roman Anthony remains in the leadoff spot and will play left field. Wilyer Abreu moves from fifth to third, while Willson Contreras stays in the cleanup spot.
Adley Rutschman drops two places in the order after batting third Tuesday. The catcher will hit fifth, followed by Caleb Durbin, Trevor Story, Kiner-Falefa and Eaton.
Red Sox Lineup Vs. Rangers
- Roman Anthony, LF
- Jahmai Jones, DH
- Wilyer Abreu, RF
- Willson Contreras, 1B
- Adley Rutschman, C
- Caleb Durbin, 3B
- Trevor Story, SS
- Isiah Kiner-Falefa, 2B
- Nate Eaton, CF
Jake Bennett will start on the mound for Boston. The left-hander enters Wednesday with a 9-7 record, a 3.69 ERA and 83 strikeouts. Gore will oppose Bennett for Texas. The Rangers left-hander is 8-11 with a 4.62 ERA and 172 strikeouts.
The matchup with Gore likely contributed to manager Chad Tracy loading the bottom half of his lineup with right-handed hitters. Jones, Contreras, Durbin, Story, Kiner-Falefa and Eaton all will bat from the right side. Boston needs a better collective offensive performance after producing only two runs in Tuesday's opener. Sogard supplied both with a two-run home run against Jacob deGrom in the third inning, but the Red Sox could not complete the comeback after falling behind 4-0.
The loss dropped Boston to 82-69 with only 11 regular-season games remaining. The Red Sox entered Wednesday 9 1/2 games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League East and 5 1/2 games behind the New York Yankees.
Wednesday's first pitch is scheduled for 8:05 p.m. ET at Globe Life Field. NESN will carry the game.

item.title: [NESN] Chad Tracy Hints Red Sox Could Call Up Triple-A Stolen Base Leader | NESN
item.dc:creator: Dan Treacy
item.description: The Red Sox are anticipating some major additions for the postseason, from the long-awaited returns of Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck to the expected activation of Ceddanne Rafaela. A prospect who has yet to debut in the majors could be nearly as impactful. Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy hinted Wednesday that speedster Braiden Ward could be called up with the postseason looming, after a dominant season on the basepaths in the minor leagues. Ward, who would have to be added to the 40-man ro
item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are anticipating some major additions for the postseason, from the long-awaited returns of Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck to the expected activation of Ceddanne Rafaela. A prospect who has yet to debut in the majors could be nearly as impactful.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy hinted Wednesday that speedster Braiden Ward could be called up with the postseason looming, after a dominant season on the basepaths in the minor leagues.
Ward, who would have to be added to the 40-man roster, would be eligible for the postseason despite spending the entire year in triple-A Worcester up to this point.
Here's more to know about Ward and his potential call-up.
Who is Braiden Ward?
Tracy told WEEI's "Rich and Ken with Ted Johnson" that Ward could be called up at some point soon. "I think that would be considered, for sure," Tracy said.
Chad Tracy on @richkented talking about potentially calling up Braiden Ward: 'I think that would be considered, for sure.'
— Rob Bradford (@bradfo) September 16, 2026
Ward is 27, which is older than a typical prospect, but he would be coming up for something that can't necessarily be taught: speed. A 16th-round pick out of Washington in 2021, Ward leads triple-A with 58 stolen bases this season and has 269 career minor-league stolen bases in 519 games.
Originally drafted by the Rockies, Ward spent four years in Colorado's system before coming over in return for reliever Brennan Bernardino in a November trade last year.
Pinch-runners can be valuable in the postseason if there is room on the roster, and a foot injury for Eli White could play a role in opening up some space for Ward even if his bat isn't much of a tool the Red Sox can use in October.
Here's a full look at Ward's minor-league stats in 2026.
Braiden Ward Minor League Stats
| Games | AVG | HR | RBI | H | SB | OPS |
| 105 | .238 | 5 | 29 | 87 | 58 | .712 |
Ward hasn't had a strong season offensively, batting .238 without flashing much power, but he still gets on base at more than a 35 percent clip and has a career .386 minor-league on base percentage in part because he has a penchant for getting hit by pitches; Ward has been hit 30 times in 2026.
If the Red Sox give Ward a chance down the stretch, it will be because of his speed. Ward's 58 stolen bases are the most in either triple-A league, and a bit of additional speed on the basepaths in the postseason, when games tend to be lower-scoring, could make a major difference for Boston.

item.content:encoded:
戻る者が増えるほど、１０月のイスは減っていく。ポストシーズン進出を目前にするレッドソックスで、最後の「野手枠」を巡る争いが一気に複雑になってきた。米老舗誌「スポーツ・イラストレイテッド」の電子版「ＯＮ ＳＩ」は１６日（日本時間１７日）、ロミー・ゴンザレス内野手（３０）の処遇に焦点を当てた。
左肩手術から６月末に復帰したものの、本人がリハビリを急ぎ過ぎたと認める中、１９試合で６５打数１２安打、打率１割８分５厘、１本塁打、ＯＰＳ０・５７２と振るわず８月４日（同５日）に３Ａへ降格。ただ、９月は３Ａで好調を維持しており、左腕に強く複数ポジションを守れる右打者として１０月の戦力に再浮上している。
同メディアは、ポストシーズンのロースターに入れるならコナー・ウォンかミッキー・ガスパー、両捕手のどちらかが押し出される可能性を指摘した。そこで忘れてならないのが、吉田正尚外野手（３３）だ。左太もも裏を痛めて８月１６日（同１７日）に１０日間の負傷者リスト（ＩＬ）へ入ったが、想定より速いペースで復帰へ向かっている。その一方、一部米メディアでは「健康でも１０月は外すべきだ」との厳しい見立ても出ている。
ただ、故障前の吉田は絶好調だった。負傷前の３３試合で打率３割２分１厘、出塁率３割７分７厘、長打率５割５厘。「落選」を当然視できる数字ではなく、短期決戦で、その打力を切り捨てるのは簡単ではない。
ゴンザレスが戻り、吉田まで間に合えば、歓迎すべき戦力回復がそのまま首脳陣の難問に変わる。誰を残し、誰を外すのか。レッドソックスの１０月は、相手との戦いを前に〝最後のイス取りゲーム〟が待っている。

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] What Red Sox Are Expected to Do With Chad Tracy, Craig Breslow
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown

item.content:encoded:
Back in April, the Boston Red Sox's season was going off the rails.
The Red Sox started the season off with a 10-17 record and opted to fire a World Series-winning manager in Alex Cora — plus a handful of other coaches — and take a gamble by turning the reins over to interim manager Chad Tracy. At the time, it seemed like the sky was falling. That's because the losses kept piling up, so much so that the Red Sox were 14 games below .500 at 32-46 on June 25.
At the time, the season looked like a disaster. The Red Sox were trending towards being sellers ahead of the trade deadline, both Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet were on the Injured List with no end in sight, and it seemed like chief baseball officer Craig Breslow's seat was getting hotter and hotter. But the Red Sox transformed their season and now, with the season winding down, ESPN's Buster Olney reported on Wednesday that the expectation is that both Breslow and Tracy will stay on with Boston beyond the 2026 season.
"But Breslow's vision of a team succeeding with pitching and defense fully manifested, and the Red Sox are closing in on a playoff berth and will likely face the Yankees in the wild-card round, again," Olney wrote. "Manager Chad Tracy has been working under an interim tag all season, something of a head-scratcher; it may be that the two sides talked about the idea of an extension in midseason but set aside the topic for the offseason. But Boston is now expected to retain both Breslow and Tracy."
The Red Sox Are Making The Right Call
This is undoubtedly the right call for the Red Sox at this time.
Let's start with Breslow. Whether you love him or not, he has built a team that can go on a run. Sure, there have been some misses over the last few years. Losing Alex Bregman was a public relations disaster. Not landing one of the big free agent bats, including Kyle Schwarber and Pete Alonso, this past offseason also was a surprise. But there are far more wins under Breslow's belt, than losses.
Sonny Gray is going to get Cy Young Award votes and has been Boston's ace this season. Ranger Suárez was an All-Star. Willson Contreras was an All-Star. Caleb Durbin is the heart and the soul of the 2026 Red Sox. Now, the Red Sox have an All-Star catcher on their hands in Adley Rutschman. Bringing back Mickey Gasper has turned into a game-changing move. And the list goes on. The Red Sox have a roster that can make noise.
On the Tracy front, there was obviously a learning curve to being a big league manager taking over during a season, especially in such a high-profile market, like Boston. He has handled the role with grace and has clearly gotten better as the year has gone on. Plus, it doesn't hurt that the Red Sox went on a historic 15-game winning streak and put together one of the best mid-season turnarounds in MLB history. All in all, these two should both be back in 2026 and it sounds like that will be the reality.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Boston Red Sox On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.content:encoded:
Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman seems to impact winning everywhere he goes.
That's one of the main reasons the Boston Red Sox wanted to re-sign the two-time World Series champion and three-time All-Star.
Bregman provided valuable veteran leadership for younger Red Sox players, like outfielder Roman Anthony.
Now, Bregman is having a similar effect with Chicago's core, specifically MVP candidate Pete Crow-Armstrong.
"In addition to the typically Bregman-esque defense at the hot corner (+8 Outs Above Average) and an OPS+ more than 20% better than league average, the Cubs’ veteran offseason addition has been lauded for his clubhouse presence," MLB.com's Anthony Castrovince wrote.
"The mentorship he provided Pete Crow-Armstrong early in the year about plate approach and swing decisions helped unleash PCA’s MVP-worthy year," Castrovince added.
Whatever Bregman told Crow-Armstrong has clearly worked.
PCA is the leading candidate for the NL MVP, hitting 42 home runs while leading the league with a .566 slugging percentage and 154 OPS+.
The outfielder's chase rate remains below league average, but PCA's improved swing decisions have helped him become one of the best hitters in baseball.
Clearly, Bregman deserves some credit for helping "unleash" one of the game's top stars.

item.title: [sportingnews.com] Red Sox have a $30 million Sonny Gray problem after 2026 season | Sporting News
item.dc:creator: Matt Sullivan

Whether it's about the future of Jarren Duran in the outfield, or how the team will handle the infield setup with Franklin Arias potentially an option, this is a very important offseason. But one of the keys to the offseason will revolve around Sonny Gray. Tim Kelly of Bleacher Report highlighted the $30 mil
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are in the middle of a postseason push this September, but one the 2026 season comes to a close, there are going to be some huge questions the Red Sox will need to answer.
Whether it's about the future of Jarren Duran in the outfield, or how the team will handle the infield setup with Franklin Arias potentially an option, this is a very important offseason. But one of the keys to the offseason will revolve around Sonny Gray.
Tim Kelly of Bleacher Report highlighted the $30 million question the Red Sox will have with Gray this fall and winter. With a $30M mutual option, the Red Sox are at real risk of losing Gray to the open market this offseason.
Red Sox facing tricky $30M Sonny Gray problem
"Considering he'll pitch next season at 37, he's probably not going to get more than $30 million for 2027 as a free agent," Kelly writes. "However, if he declines the option, the Red Sox will owe him a $10 million buyout."
Boston is surely going to accept their side of the $30 million mutual option, considering how great Gray has been for the Red Sox this season.
But when it comes to whether Gray will accept the option or not, this $10 million buyout presents a big problem for the Red Sox.
It would not be a surprise if Gray declined the option, got the $10M buyout from the Red Sox, and then sought out a $20 million per-year contract.
Even though Gray is older, some team, whether it's the Red Sox or another club, will surely be willing to spend $20 million to land Gray.
But what makes it so tricky is that Gray could sign a two-year, $40 million deal on the open market, guaranteeing he lands an extra $20 million in 2028, regardless of his performance and health during the 2027 season.
He has a 2.76 ERA and a 17-5 record with the Red Sox in 2026, and is deserving of a big contract if he hits the open market. Even though he's older, his incredible 2026 season could present a challenge for the Red Sox.
Teams are going to have interest in Gray, and his $30 million option presents a big problem for the Red Sox. They could be out a key starter and lose some money in the process. This is a tricky situation, and one Craig Breslow needs to manage well.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox could have a slew of pitching reinforcements returning before the playoffs begin, including Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, and maybe even Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford. Justin Slaten will not be among them.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy on September 15 told reporters (including Tim Healey of The Boston Globe) that Slaten got a PRP injection in his arm to address a flexor issue. His season is over after multiple attempts to ramp up for a rehab assignment and eventual return.
Slaten has been quite injury prone over his three years with the Red Sox. He went on the injured list for the first time this season in early April and didn't return until mid-May. For the second straight year, he'll finish his season with less than 35 innings pitched.
Justin Slaten's season with Red Sox ends after he gets PCP injection for flexor injury
The righty has dabbled in the extremes this season, finishing with a 4.60 ERA over 31.1 innings. In June, Slaten's worst month this year, he allowed nine runs on 17 hits over 11 outings. July was his best, during which he let up just one run on five hits over nine appearances. His WHIP has starkly increased over the past year, from 1.09 in 2025 to 1.37.
When the Red Sox can get Slaten's best, he's one of the biggest threats out of their bullpen. But he's often injured or prone to blowups that keep him from showing the best he can offer. It will be interesting to see his role next season when Boston has more healthy pitching depth it could push to the bullpen.
Red Sox confirm Kristian Campbell's season is over due to foot injury, ending breakout
Kristian Campbell's season has also ended prematurely due to an injury. The outfielder will be out for the rest of the year due to a left foot contusion, according to Tommy Cassell of the Worcester Telegram & Gazette.
The WooSox pulled Campbell from their September 8 game due to the injury. Even before the announcement of his IL stint, it was evident that Campbell's season could be over, as Worcester's last regular season game is on Septembet 20.
Campbell's injury ends a resurgent second half for the 24 year old. He slashed .311/.430/.497 over 51 games after the All-Star break and, had he been healthy, he might've been selected to come up and help the major league team while Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White are injured.
Romy Gonzalez continues tear following arm injury scare with WooSox
On the same day Campbell was pulled from the WooSox's lineup, Romy Gonzalez was, too. An arm injury led to a week on the shelf for the utility infielder, but he joined the Triple-A lineup again on September 15.
Gonzalez has resumed the tear he was on before his arm flared up. He logged two hits, including a double, in his return and boosted his September slash line to .500/.520/.727 over six games. Gonzalez has hit so well lately that it could be time to call him back up to the major leagues to give Boston's slumping offense a boost.

I’m not su
item.content:encoded:
This morning, we asked whether the Red Sox were ready to give Romy Gonzalez another chance. From his point of view, he’s ready to go. After acknowledging that his initial rehab was rushed in an attempt to get back on the field, he now says “I’m ready whenever my name’s called… I’ve always been extremely confident in what I can do… I think I’ve showed that over the past two seasons.” (Christopher Smith, MassLive)
Speaking of rehabbing power-hitting infielders, what’s Curtis Mead up to?
I’m not sure “light” tee work at this stage is going to have him ready for the postseason in time, but you never know.
Unfortunately there’s one player who definitely won’t return from injury in time. Justin Slaten, who was initially on the IL with elbow inflammation, has been shut down for the season. Moreover, it looks like the issue might be more serious than initially thought. “There’s some degenerative changes in the flexor mass,” Chad Tracy said. “So that’s substantially different news.” He’ll receive a plasma injection to stimulate healing, and, unfortunately, this sounds like something that could require surgery eventually. (Hayden Bird, Boston.com)
Things are progressing for Garrett Crochet, though. He threw thirty pitches over two simulated innings yesterday. “Everything went well,” Chad Tracy said. “That was the most volume he’s had, so we’ll see over the next couple of days how he feels and go from there.” (Tim Healey, Boston Globe)
Hopefully Crochet can work his way back like Trevor Story, who is well aware that he has doubters amongst the Red Sox fanbase and media. “You see a lot of that stuff, but I really try to channel it into an energy in a way that I can use,” he said. “At the time, I wasn’t trying to pay much attention to it, but people would bring it to me, and I decided how I was going to look at it. I just tried to channel it into when I do come back, and it’s all about the playoffs, and it’s all about winning this thing at the end. That’s where I put my energy and focus.” (Jen McCaffrey, The Athletic)

item.description: Alex and Reagan Bregman are still one of baseball’s recognizable couples, with Alex’s long MLB career providing the foundation for their household wealth. item.content:encoded:
Alex and Reagan Bregman are still one of baseball’s recognizable couples, with Alex’s long MLB career providing the foundation for their household wealth. Alex’s financial story took a new turn in 2026 when he signed with the Chicago Cubs after nine seasons with the Houston Astros and one with the Boston Red Sox.
The couple’s financial profile goes further than just Alex Bregman’s playing salary. The family has also been involved in other business and commercial ventures, and Reagan Bregman has gone into entrepreneurship, including with her Exiza activewear brand. Figures for public net worth will vary between sources, so estimates should be regarded as approximations and not as confirmed financial statements.
Alex Bregman and Reagan Bregman combined net worth in 2026
Alex Bregman is the biggest part of the couple's publicly estimated wealth. Sports Illustrated estimated his net worth at around $107.8 million in January 2026, citing baseball salary, endorsements and business ventures as the primary sources of his fortune; this figure does not necessarily indicate the combined net worth of the couple.
Celebrity Net Worth reports that his finances took a turn for the better when he signed a five-year, $175 million contract with the Chicago Cubs in January of 2026.
Celebrity Net Worth notes that the average value of the deal is $35 million a year, but there's $70 million deferred, so the headline value of the contract and the immediate cash flow are not the same thing.
| Financial area | Alex Bregman | Reagan Bregman |
| Main income sources | MLB salary, endorsements, businesses | Entrepreneurship and business ventures |
| 2026 team/business connection | Chicago Cubs | Exiza and other ventures |
| Public net-worth estimate | About $107.8 million | Not reliably disclosed |
| Major financial development | $175 million Cubs contract | Independent entrepreneurial career |
Alex Bregman’s Chicago Cubs contract boosts household wealth
The biggest known new financial commitment tied to the household in 2026 is Alex Bregman's deal with the Chicago Cubs. Celebrity Net Worth reports that the five-year deal is worth $175 million, the largest average annual salary in Chicago Cubs history at $35 million per season.
Celebrity Net Worth reports that the deal also includes $70 million in deferred compensation. This structure allows for some of the contractual value to be paid later, not all during the five-year playing period; the contract should therefore be seen as a long-term financial asset and not just $175 million in immediate earnings.
Bregman made a lot of MLB money during his tenure with the Houston Astros and Boston Red Sox before coming to Chicago. He has made plenty of money as a player already, as evidenced by the $138.44 million in salary through the end of 2025 reported by Sports Illustrated, even before the deal with the Cubs.
Reagan Bregman’s businesses add to family income
Reagan Bregman has found a professional identity of her own alongside Alex Bregman’s baseball career. PEOPLE notes that she’s the founder of Exiza, a Houston-based ethical athleisure brand she started in 2021, which gives her an independent entrepreneurial platform outside of being an MLB player’s wife.
She’s also been at Google for many years before changing to entrepreneurship and family life. Reagan spoke about leaving Google after nearly a decade and then launching her own business in a 2026 interview with PEOPLE.
Alex Bregman has a lucrative pay cheque in MLB and endorsements, but Reagan Bregman has her own entrepreneurial ventures and makes her own money from various streams. Alex’s baseball contract alone doesn’t determine the Bregmans’ lifestyle and net worth, and their exact combined net worth isn’t known without private financials.

item.content:encoded:
After a brief demotion, Greg Weissert has served an important role in the Boston bullpen.
After a historic July that saw the Boston Red Sox use high-leverage arms on a near-nightly basis, one of baseball's best bullpens became injury-ravaged, losing Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, and Justin Slaten to fatigue-related injuries. The losses of Whitlock, Slaten, and Guerrero forced interim manager Chad Tracy to turn to other relievers in high-leverage spots. Among those arms is right-hander Greg Weissert, who, after a brief trip to Triple-A Worcester, has come up huge for the bullpen.
In his first 48 appearances of the season, Weissert posted a 3.97 ERA in 45.1 innings pitched. The 31-year-old right-hander struggled in particular when taking over in situations with men already on base, allowing 13 of 29 inherited runners to score, which, at the time, was the third-most among all relievers.
After needing 34 pitches to get through an inning in Boston's 13-inning marathon win over the Chicago White Sox on Aug. 6, Weissert fell victim to the numbers game, getting optioned to Triple-A Worcester on Aug. 7 in favor of a fresher arm. However, it wound up being just a six-day trip as he was recalled on Aug. 13 when the team placed Whitlock on the IL.
In 12 appearances since being recalled, Weissert has more than made up for the losses of Whitlock, who returned on Aug. 29, Guerrero, who is slated to return ahead of Wednesday's game in Texas and Slaten. He's allowed only two earned runs on 11 hits, striking out 13 and walking only four in 10.2 innings of work. Most importantly, Weissert has performed much better when entering 'dirty' innings, allowing only one of seven inherited runners to score.
Despite Whitlock's return and Guerrero's imminent return, Weissert's reemergence as a reliable option will help in the final 11 games of the regular season and the postseason run, as Tracy announced Tuesday that Slaten will not return in 2026 after undergoing a PRP injection in his right elbow to treat degenerative changes in his flexor mass.
Up next for the Sox
After falling 4-2 in Tuesday night's series opener against the Texas Rangers, the Red Sox will look to even up the series in game two of three from Globe Life Field on Wednesday night. Rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite fellow southpaw MacKenzie Gore (8-11, 4.62 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
Postseason baseball is right around the corner, which means it’s time to analyze a certain starting pitcher who seems to have American League Cy Young honors pretty much wrapped up with a bow.
I’m talking about New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler, who’s in the midst of an incredibly successful second season in the majors and looks like he’ll be a force in the league for a long time.
After former Detroit Tigers star Tarik Skubal walked away with the American League Cy Young in both 2024 and 2025, Schlittler is looking to assert himself as the new frontline pitcher in the American League. Let’s just say if Skubal didn’t get traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers and still remained on the Detroit Tigers, Schlittler probably still would have the upper hand, which is pretty impressive.
Other elite arms like Dylan Cease, Parker Messick, Drew Rasmussen and Reid Detmers have certainly given him a run for his money, but Schlittler is likely to take home the hardware when it’s all said and done.
He is also looking to be the Yankees’ second Cy Young Award winner in the last four years. Gerrit Cole took home the honors in 2023 after his excellent campaign, in which he owned a 2.63 ERA and 0.98 WHIP. Schlittler’s 2026 campaign has actually been even better.
Now that everything has been set up, it’s time to dig deeper into what has fueled Schlittler’s elite 2026 campaign.
*Stats pulled from games completed through September 14.
Schlittler Came Out of the Blue, Kind Of
Up until the 2025 season, most people probably didn’t even know who Cam Schlittler was and what organization he was a part of. He was drafted by the Yankees in the seventh round of the 2022 draft out of Northeastern University.
He was an all-around solid pitcher in college over his three seasons, posting a 2.62 ERA and 1.08 WHIP, with 30 out of his 31 appearances being starts.
Schlittler didn’t make his affiliated debut within the Yankees system until the 2023 season and showed mixed results between rookie ball, Single-A, and High-A.
Even though he struck out a lot of batters and kept home runs to a minimum, he issued a lot of walks, which inflated his surface numbers.
Over the next two years spanning the 2024 and 2025 seasons, he gradually made his way through the Yankees’ minor league system and started to show some solid improvements.
By the time the 2025 campaign rolled around, Schlittler found himself on MLB Pipeline’s list of the Yankees’ top 30 prospects for the first time, being slotted in at number 12.
He was mowing down hitters, limiting walks, limiting home runs and was simply putting it all together between Double-A and Triple-A.
| Season | HR/9 | BB/9 | K/9 |
| 2023 | 0.8 | 4.1 | 9.8 |
| 2024 | 0.7 | 4.1 | 11.5 |
| 2025 | 0.5 | 3.1 | 11.6 |
Schlittler’s excellent performance was evident to the Yankees front office, and the organization decided it was time to give him a shot at the major league level. Let’s just say it’s been stunning to see what he’s been able to accomplish so quickly.
Pure Dominance in the Majors
Now that I’ve highlighted Schlittler’s underlooked journey to the big leagues, hopefully you’ll appreciate his insane numbers a little more and notice how far he has come along in terms of development.
He had a nice cup of tea with the Yankees in 2025 after he debuted on July 9, finishing the season with an excellent 2.96 ERA and 1.22 WHIP spanning a stretch of 14 starts. A majority of his growth in the minor leagues had carried over to the majors, which was really encouraging to see.
Last year, Schlittler gave us a little glimpse into what he’d provide long term, but no one realized what kind of pitching monster he’d turn into presently in 2026.
You could even argue that he’s been better than Jacob Misiorowski because their numbers have pretty much been identical, give or take. That means you could argue he’s the best pitcher in the majors currently.
So far in 2026, across 31 starts and 184.2 innings pitched, Schlittler has shown pure dominance, pitching to a superb 1.95 ERA and 0.90 WHIP. His ratios have been really good, as backed up by his excellent 6 H/9, 0.8 HR/9, 2.1 BB/9 and 11.1 K/9.
Schlittler currently leads the American League with 5.9 fWAR. He ranks second overall, only trailing Misirowski, who has been worth 6.0 fWAR.
His underlying peripherals look great, including his 2.87 xERA and 2.57 FIP. That is a result of his ability to limit dangerous contact and total baserunners via low hit and walk rates, as previously mentioned.
In terms of pitching run value calculated by Baseball Savant, Schlittler ranks fourth in the majors, currently worth +38 runs. He trails only Yoshinobu Yamamoto (39), Dylan Cease (39) and Jacob Misiorowski (47).
The reason as to why his pitching run value is so high is because of how effective his pitch arsenal has been. Schlittler primarily works with four quality pitches: a four-seam fastball (44%), cutter (25%), sinker (20%) and curveball (10%).
The fastball combo of his four-seam and sinker has been lethal and goes to show how important and effective tunneling can be.
Schlittler’s fastball, which averages 98 mph, is worth a +27 run value, and batters have only managed a .164 batting average and .230 wOBA against the offering. His counterpart 97.8 mph sinker is being valued at a +11 run value, with a .172 batting average and .266 xwOBA.
Also note that Schlittler has 6.8 feet of extension, which places him in the 81st percentile. This helps create a faster perceived velocity for an already powerful fastball mix.
His cutter, which averages 94.7 mph, has been a hint above average with a +1 run value, while his 86.3 mph curveball has been his worst and least-used pitch, worth -1 in run value. If Schlittler can improve just one of those pitches, it could be wraps for his opponents.
Schlittler’s stuff has been very good, to say the least, and batters are having a really hard time making contact on his offerings. His current 34.2% chase rate ranks in the 85th percentile, while his 29.1% whiff rate ranks in the 79th percentile.
Despite the fact that opponents are making limited contact with Schlittler’s offerings, they still have managed to make decent contact when they do connect.
This is one of the few flaws in Schlittler’s already great profile that could use some improvement. Opponents have managed a 7.7% barrel rate (45th percentile) and 39.1% hard-hit (44th percentile) rate against him. Those numbers aren’t bad, but they could be better.
Will Schlittler Take Home AL Cy Young Honors?
Plain and simple, Schlittler has been dominant. And there’s actually a good chance he gets even better down the road based on what we’ve looked at.
It seems very likely that Schlittler will be named the 2026 American League Cy Young when it’s all said and done. Cease has pleaded his case in the best way he’s able to, but all signs are pointing to Schlittler.
Simply just looking at Schlittler’s and Cease’s second-half splits pretty much ends the conversation.
Yordan Alvarez seems like the leading candidate for American League Most Valuable Player, but you’d think Schlittler will be considered there as well. Alvarez leads all AL batters with 5.8 fWAR, but Schlittler does have him topped with 5.9 fWAR — something to keep an eye out for.
We’ll have to wait and see what happens, but Schlittler looks to have wrapped up the conversation for the American League Cy Young.

item.dc:creator: Scott Roche

item.content:encoded:
When the Boston Red Sox made some additions to their starting rotation last winter, they were hoping to rebuild it around ace Garrett Crochet. Little did they know that making those moves would turn out to be monster moves.
After losing out on Alex Bregman in free agency to the Chicago Cubs, Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow pivoted to pitching. He signed left-hander Ranger Suárez of the Philadelphia Phillies. Earlier in the offseason, Breslow acquired veteran Sonny Gray from the St. Louis Cardinals.
That is turning into the biggest offseason addition made by Boston. He is going to finish at least in the top 5 in the American League Cy Young voting, but will be a free agent following the season with an option for 2027. Breslow and Gray will have a decision to make this winter, according to Kerry Miller of Bleacher Report.
Boston Red Sox Facing Sonny Gray Decision This Winter
When decisions are to be made for 2027, Gray has a mutual option of $30 million. Now, whether or not Gray plays next season remains to be seen, according to Alex Speier of the Boston Globe.
“If my family wants me to hang it up, I’ll be done in a heartbeat,” Gray said, per Speier.
If they don’t want him to retire, the Red Sox would love to have him back. He is 17-5 in his first season in Boston with a 2.76 ERA in 27 starts. He has been a workhorse in 156.2 innings with 140 strikeouts. Gray has struggled in recent outings. However, he is still on track to get the ball in Game 1 of the AL wild-card series.
“Even with major money committed to Ranger Suárez and Garrett Crochet in the rotation already, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow will probably pick up the team’s half of the option,” Miller wrote.
“The question is whether Gray will. Considering he’ll pitch next season at 37, he’s probably not going to get more than $30 million for 2027 as a free agent. However, if he declines the option, the Red Sox will owe him a $10 million buyout. So he could collect that buyout, try to get at least $20 million for 2027, and perhaps pursue a multi-year commitment. He has plenty to consider.”
Crochet has been out injured for a majority of this season and is looking for a postseason return. Suárez has been better in his last couple of starts in September.
Boston Red Sox Facing Key Offseason Decision
Gray is scheduled to make his next start on Thursday night against the Texas Rangers in Arlington. Then he’ll get one more next week before his start in the wild-card round. Depending on how far the Red Sox go, all eyes could turn to 2027.
Boston’s rotation next season, if healthy when the season begins, with Gray, could be one of the top ones in the American League. If there is any question as to whether or not Gray has another year left in him, that should have been answered by his 2026 season.
There are some big decisions coming for Breslow this winter. Gray is going to be at the top of that list.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] What Garrett Crochet Injury Update Means for Red Sox
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: Garrett Crochet is looming over the Boston Red Sox's playoff push, despite the fact that he hasn't taken the hill in a big league game since April 25. At this point, a new update seems to surface in Crochet's attempted return to game action every few days. And all of them have been positive, to say the least. On Tuesday, Crochet threw another bullpen and tossed his most pitches yet (30) en route back to Boston, per The Boston Globe's Tim Healey. "Garrett Crochet’s two-inning, 30-pitch bullpen se
item.content:encoded:
Garrett Crochet is looming over the Boston Red Sox's playoff push, despite the fact that he hasn't taken the hill in a big league game since April 25.
At this point, a new update seems to surface in Crochet's attempted return to game action every few days. And all of them have been positive, to say the least. On Tuesday, Crochet threw another bullpen and tossed his most pitches yet (30) en route back to Boston, per The Boston Globe's Tim Healey.
"Garrett Crochet’s two-inning, 30-pitch bullpen session — his heaviest workload so far — went well today, Chad Tracy said. He’ll rest for a couple of days. Sounds like he still won’t be getting into a Triple-A game before that season ends Sunday," Healey wrote.
Garrett Crochet Is Getting Closer
There's a lot to take away from this update for the big lefty. First and foremost, the fact that he's been able to continue throwing and building up is a huge positive. In his last outing on Friday, Crochet tossed just over 20 pitches and introduced his sweeper into the mix. Now, a few days later, he's up to 30 pitches and also an up-and-down. The up-and-down is important in itself. That's a simulation of game action. If Crochet does return to game action before the 2026 season comes to an end, it's going to be in a bullpen role.
He's not coming back to be the starter Boston fans have seen, but instead hopefully a multi-inning weapon to take the bullpen to an even higher level. Now, the next step is going to be seeing how he reacts to the starting and stopping of the up-and-down. If he comes away feeling good, it will be massive for his chances of a return.
The fact that Healey reported that it doesn't sound like Crochet will pitch in Triple-A before Worcester's season comes to a close isn't shocking. In early September, it was shared that Crochet was trending towards a return for the postseason, even if he doesn't go on a rehab assignment beforehand. So, this already has been an idea out there.
When it comes to Crochet, the biggest thing to watch now is when he will face live batters. That's the next significant step. The second the Red Sox have him facing live hitters, that will be the next big step in his recovery. Crochet is close. He has thrown a handful of bullpens already and now he has an up-and-down under his belt. The Red Sox will begin a Wild Card round series on Sep. 29. That's 13 days away, as of writing. It's still very possible for Crochet to provide some much-needed help for this bullpen.

But, as far as the Triple-A club is concerned, few guys (I know, I know, Franklin Arias might be one) have had as many big moments as Allan Castro. This wasn’t the 23-year-old’s strongest season from an OPS standpoint, but the big moments are getting notable. item.content:encoded:
The WooSox roster has a bunch of guys who’ve made some plays for the Major League roster this season. But, as far as the Triple-A club is concerned, few guys (I know, I know, Franklin Arias might be one) have had as many big moments as Allan Castro. This wasn’t the 23-year-old’s strongest season from an OPS standpoint, but the big moments are getting notable. He just had a go-ahead home run the other day and he’s had multiple other walkoffs throughout the season. Yesterday, the WooSox again started a series on the winning side due to his bat, as he hit a 2-out single to score the Manfred runner. And, yes, in the process of all of this, Franklin Arias got himself a knock as did Romy Gonzalez. (Here’s that Castro hit.)
The game in general was a defensive battle. The Durham Bulls (Rays AAA) had the benefit of up-and-down starter Mason Englart dealing on Tuesday night as they couldn’t get on the board until Englart departed after seven. Luckily, Jedixson Paez was just as hot even without some of the strikeout numbers. His only run allowed was via a home run way back on the second at-bat of the game, and the 22-year-old righty recovered wonderfully from that, retiring fifteen consecutive Durham batters. From there, Tanner Houck came in and struck out the side in his rehab appearance, and it is starting to look likely that he sees some innings in a relief capacity as the Red Sox’s magic number dwindles. Osvaldo Berrios and Hobie Harris would then slam the door even in the face of a few more Bulls scoring opportunities; the WooSox had the only opportunity with runners in scoring position of the game. Enter extra innings, and enter Castro’s sealing single. Game over, 2-1.

item.title: [Boston.com] Red Sox reliever Justin Slaten set to miss rest of season
item.dc:creator: Hayden Bird
item.description: Justin Slaten’s injury: The Red Sox bullpen got a dose of bad news earlier this week when it was learned that reliever Justin Slaten — who has been out since Aug. 16 with what was initially called right elbow inflammation — is now likely to miss the rest of the season. item.content:encoded:
Justin Slaten’s injury: The Red Sox bullpen got a dose of bad news earlier this week when it was learned that reliever Justin Slaten — who has been out since Aug. 16 with what was initially called right elbow inflammation — is now likely to miss the rest of the season.
Interim manager Chad Tracy spoke to reporters about the matter on Tuesday, acknowledging that the injury is worse than what was originally thought. Slaten, 29, saw well respected orthopedic and sports medicine surgeon Keith Meister in Arlington, Texas prior to the team’s series against the Rangers, and was diagnosed with a more problematic issue.
“There’s some degenerative changes in the flexor mass,” Tracy explained, via Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. “So that’s substantially different news.”
Along with an injection of injection of platelet-rich plasma, Slaten will continue to rest. His status for the remainder of the 2026 season, already up in the air, now appears to be settled.
“This maybe adds some finality to the fact,” Tracy said of Slaten being out. “We were already operating that way, but you still held out hope.
“It’s a big loss — at least now, the finality of knowing we can’t have it back,” Tracy concluded.
Slaten had a 4.60 ERA in 31.1 innings in 2026 (36 appearances). His loss will be partly offset by the expected return this week of fellow reliever Tyson Guerrero, who has been on the injured list since Sept 1.
Trivia: What Red Sox pitcher holds the team’s single-season record for appearances?
(Answer at the bottom).
Hint: He did it in 2005 (81 total appearances), and won four World Series titles in his career (two in Boston, two in Toronto).
More from Boston.com:
Out of the ballpark in a hurry: Though it proved to be not enough for a win on Tuesday, Nick Sogard hit a line drive home run that left the yard at high speed.
On this day: On the same day that the struggling Red Sox fired general manager Mike “Pinky” Higgins, Boston right-hander Dave Morehead threw a no-hitter in front of just 1,247 fans at Fenway Park. Morehead’s heroics helped the Red Sox defeat future Boston ace Luis Tiant and Cleveland by a 2-0 final score. It would be the last Red Sox no-hitter until Hideo Nomo in 2001.
Daily highlight: An absolute missile from Liverpool midfielder Dominik Szoboszlai helped ensure a win (3-1) over Tottenham in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday.
Trivia answer: Mike Timlin

The Red Sox (82-69) currently hold the second wild-card spot in the American League. This season, Slaten (2-4) had a 4.60 ERA with 39 strikeouts in 31 1/3 innings.

Jones was a platoon revelation when he first arrived in Boston, but he's cooled off since then (a .200 batting average over his last 12 games), and his positional inflexibility makes him a diffic
item.content:encoded:
Good morning! Last night, Chad Tracy gave at-bats to two pinch-hitters in the 8th inning: lefty killer Jahmai Jones and utility infielder Andruw Monasterio. Jones did his job in the 8th, singling to start the inning in place of Mickey Gasper, but would subsequently strike out to end the game in the 9th. Jones was a platoon revelation when he first arrived in Boston, but he's cooled off since then (a .200 batting average over his last 12 games), and his positional inflexibility makes him a difficult roster fit. Monasterio did not do his job last night. He struck out with the bases loaded, putting an end to the biggest threat the Sox had all night.
In light of last night's events it's time to ask: Is it time for Romy Gonzalez to get another crack? Romy theoretically combines the best of both Jones and Monasterio — he's a lefty-killer and a utility infielder. He struggled mightily in his (rushed) return to the Sox earlier this year and has recently been battling a nagging injury lately, but his AAA line reads .344/.400/.505 with 3 homers and 6 doubles. He could inject some pop just as the Sox look like they could use a little extra juice.
Use this space to talk about bench bats and whatever else you want, and, as always, be good to one another.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox got some bad news on Tuesday. Top prospect Kristian Campbell is going on the IL, which means his season is over.
Campbell was with the Worcester Red Sox at the Triple-A level. There, he suffered a foot contusion, per Tommy Cassell.
In 109 games with the WooSox, Campbell has a .256 average this season with a .763 OPS. That’s with 8 home runs, 51 RBIs, and 73 walks. Defensively, he’s spent most of his time in the outfield. That’s despite largely playing second base in 2025.
Notably, Campbell was showing improvement in the second half. In 36 games since the All-Star break, he was hitting .333 with a 1.009 OPS, to go along with 6 home runs. That had, seemingly, made him an option to come up to the majors.
Kristian Campbell Didn’t Play for the Boston Red Sox in 2026
In 2025, Kristian Campbell made the Boston Red Sox roster coming out of Spring Training. He was the Opening Day second baseman, and there was a lot of excitement about what he could end up being.
Things didn’t work out. In 67 games, he hit .223 with a .664 OPS. Campbell had 6 home runs and 21 RBIs. To go along with those offensive struggles, he was a bit of a liability defensively at second base. So, the Red Sox would often play him in the outfield, but they already have a logjam of players there.
Eventually, Campbell was sent to Triple-A to work on improving his swing and to find a defensive position. That’s where he’d spend the entire season.
At the MLB level, the Red Sox have had some injury issues. That’s forced them, at times, to lean on players who would normally be bench players or borderline players between Triple-A and the majors. However, they resisted rushing Campbell back to Boston, after seemingly rushing him in 2025. With his improving bat as of late, there was some excitement that he could be returning to the majors soon, but that’s not going to happen now.
The Future for the Red Sox and Campbell
While it may seem strange for Campbell to be away from the MLB team for so long, his future with the Red Sox is still bright.
Campbell is finishing up his age 24 season. He’s still relatively young and when he does get his next chance with the Red Sox, he’ll better know what to expect at the MLB level, and he’ll be going to that level with more development under his belt.
The Red Sox and Campbell are also committed to one another. In April of 2025, the Red Sox signed Campbell to an eight-year, $60 million contract. So, he’s going to be with Boston for the foreseeable future, regardless of the upcoming CBA changes.
The challenge now for Boston is to find what position Campbell will play when he rejoins the MLB team. There’s still a logjam in the outfield. Campbell still isn’t viewed as a great option defensively, and those infield spots are filling quickly. So, will a move be made to clear space for Campbell?

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Red Sox Have Awkward Roster Decision Looming With Romy Gonzalez
item.dc:creator: Jackson Roberts; Unknown

Now, with the playoffs looming, it's become difficult to see where he fits into the picture. Having been demoted to Triple-A on Aug. 4, Gonzalez has been patiently waiting his turn. The Red Sox are used to having at least one right-handed bat on the roster who primarily gets his looks against left-handed pitchers, but Jahmai Jones has usurped that role from Gonzalez at least temporarily. With 14 pos
item.content:encoded:
Romy Gonzalez seemed like a staple of the Boston Red Sox's offensive attack plan just a year ago. Now, with the playoffs looming, it's become difficult to see where he fits into the picture.
Having been demoted to Triple-A on Aug. 4, Gonzalez has been patiently waiting his turn. The Red Sox are used to having at least one right-handed bat on the roster who primarily gets his looks against left-handed pitchers, but Jahmai Jones has usurped that role from Gonzalez at least temporarily.
With 14 position players on the current active roster and likely 14 joining the Red Sox for the American League Wild Card Series in two weeks, there's an interesting conversation to have about Gonzalez now that the 30-year-old is having a hot month of September in Triple-A. Where will that conversation lead?
Is Gonzalez a legitimate threat to crack playoff roster?
Gonzalez batted near the top of the order for the Red Sox down the stretch last year whenever there was a lefty on the mound. But he also turned out to be battling a shoulder injury that necessitated surgery at the beginning of spring training and delayed his return to the majors until the end of June.
When he did make his season debut, Gonzalez recently admitted that he rushed his rehab, which might reasonably have thrown his swing out of whack against major league quality pitching. He went 12-for-65 with only one home run and a .572 OPS in his 19 major league games before his demotion.
“Where the team was at and all the injuries we had, it was my plan to kind of rush back and be up there,” Gonzalez said, via Christopher Smith of MassLive. “Obviously, hindsight’s 20/20.”
Now, with the Triple-A season coming to an end this weekend, Gonzalez has to know he might not make it back to the majors at all. But he's got the right attitude about the entire situation, seemingly.
“I’m ready whenever my name’s called,” Gonzalez said, per Smith.
If the Red Sox were going to put Gonzalez on the playoff roster, he'd likely have to displace either Connor Wong or Mickey Gasper. Nate Eaton, the current odd man out, should be replaced by Ceddanne Rafaela by the end of the week.
Jackson Roberts is a former Division III All-Region DH who now writes and talks about sports for a living. A Bay Area native and a graduate of Swarthmore College and the Newhouse School at Syracuse University, Jackson makes his home in North Jersey. He grew up rooting for the Red Sox, Patriots, and Warriors, and he recently added the Devils to his sports fandom mosaic. Crochet (shoulder) threw a 30-pitch bullpen session at Fenway Park on Tuesday, Perla Paredes of MLB.com reports.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy indicated the session went well, but the team will wait to see how Crochet responds Wednesday before determining the left-hander's next step. He's been building up his pitch count and intensity while introducing offspeed and breaking stuff during side sessions leading up to Tuesday's effort. Crochet is attempting to rejoin Boston as a reliever over the final days of the regular season.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Where Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease Sits in Latest American League Cy Young Poll
item.dc:creator: Zion Trammel; Unknown
item.description: Dylan Cease's first season with the Toronto Blue Jays has been tremendous. He rewarded the front office's confidence after signing a lucrative contract this offseason. Every team needs an ace. Cease assumed that role and took off with it. In the middle of a tight playoff race, the Blue Jays feel comfortable when the 30-year-old takes the mound. item.content:encoded:
Dylan Cease's first season with the Toronto Blue Jays has been tremendous. He rewarded the front office's confidence after signing a lucrative contract this offseason.
Every team needs an ace. Cease assumed that role and took off with it. In the middle of a tight playoff race, the Blue Jays feel comfortable when the 30-year-old takes the mound. Since the All-Star break, Toronto is 7-4 when Cease pitches.
He's accomplished a lot of firsts this season, but could he add one more to the list?
Can Cease Win His First Cy Young?
Cease has been a strikeout machine since entering the league. He's eclipsed 200+ strikeouts for six consecutive seasons, and this year, he has a new career-high of 236 strikeouts and counting.
Now, Cease has his eyes set on his first American League Cy Young Award. In 2022, he was the runner-up to Justin Verlander, who won the award unanimously. In 2024, Cease finished fourth behind Paul Skenes (3), Zack Wheeler (2), and Chris Sale (1).
This could be his best chance yet. Jared Greenspan of MLB.com laid out the latest A.L. Cy Young poll. Cease finished second behind New York Yankees pitcher Cam Schlittler. Cease received 126 points and Schlittler received 160 points.
Comparing Cease and Schlittler
Schlittler: 14-6, 184.2 IP, 1.95 ERA, 0.90 WHIP, 228 SO, 44 BB
Cease: 11-5, 166.1 IP, 2.38 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 236 SO, 72 BB
While this may be Cease's best chance, those statistics suggest it will be tough to defeat Schlittler. The righty would have to put up incredible numbers over his final three or four starts, and Schlittler would need to go in the opposite direction.
The majority of Cease's advanced metrics rank in the 90th percentile or higher on Baseball Savant. His average exit velocity (85.6), whiff percentage (33.4), strikeout percentage (35.3), and hard-hit percentage (31.9) are some of the best in baseball this year.
Cease became the first Blue Jays pitcher to start the All-Star Game since Roy Halladay in 2009. It's incredible to think this was Cease's first All-Star nod. He would become the first Toronto pitcher to win the Cy Young Award. Two have won the award this century (Robbie Ray, 2021, and Roy Halladay, 2009).
Regardless of what happens, no one can take away the brilliant year Cease has had. The talent was always there. It was about finding the right organization to unlock it. The Blue Jays became the place where Cease could thrive.
Zion Trammell graduated from TCU in 2023 with a degree in sports broadcasting and journalism. He currently writes for TCU Horned Frogs on SI. In addition to writing, he is the play-by-play voice for Southlake Carroll baseball and hosts a TCU show on the Bleav Network.
Follow zion_trammell

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Justin Slaten's Injury Costs Red Sox Dearly With Playoffs Looming
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: Over the last few weeks, or so, it has seemed like pretty much every injury update for the Boston Red Sox has been positive. item.content:encoded:
Over the last few weeks, or so, it has seemed like pretty much every injury update for the Boston Red Sox has been positive.
Garrett Crochet has been throwing, Tanner Houck has been on a rehab assignment and even Curtis Mead has been playing catch, among others. While this is the case, the Red Sox gave a negative update on Wednesday. Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy shared that reliever Justin Slaten is dealing with "degenerative changes in the flexor mass" and is likely done for the 2026 season.
"Slaten, we got ... he went and saw [Dr. Keith Meister] with our medical staff today and there's some degenerative changes in the flexor mass," Tracy said. "So he's going to be down. He's going to get a PRP injection and it's likely going to end his season. So, that's substantially different news, as far as these guys."
Bad News For Boston
This is a brutal blow for Slaten, and the Red Sox's bullpen in general. Slaten is one of the club's key high-leverage guys, but Boston hasn't had him on the mound since Aug. 12. He was initially placed on the Injured List due to right elbow inflammation. He actually started throwing, but he had to be shut down when the same "symptoms" that landed him on the Injured List popped up again.
Slaten had a 4.60 ERA in 36 appearances, but this doesn't tell the full story about why he's a big loss for Boston. In his final 17 appearances of the season, he had a 2.45 ERA and a 19-to-3 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 14 2/3 innings pitched. The first half of the season wasn't great for him, but he had turned things around and looked like the guy Boston hoped it would have out of the bullpen.
The Red Sox have just 11 games left in the 2026 regular season. Losing Slaten hurts Boston's playoff chances. On the bright side, the Red Sox's bullpen could still get better with Houck on a minor league rehab assignment and Garrett Crochet throwing as well. With Slaten likely out for the season, that's one less change Boston will have to make when building the playoff roster. Tyron Guerrero, Crochet, and Houck are all inching their way back. Boston will have to clear three spots to get these guys on the roster. That could be bad news for guys like Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, and Raymond Burgos, among others.
With Slaten likely not coming back, it's one less decision for Boston to make. Of course, it would be better if he were returning, but that isn't the case right now. Unfortunately, Red Sox fans have seemingly seen the last of Slaten for the 2026 season.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Boston Red Sox On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Jake Bennett is pitching his way off the Red Sox's playoff rotation as struggles mount
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello
item.description: Jake Bennett might not be Garrett Crochet, but the 25-year-old rookie has done an admirable job this season filling in for the injured Boston Red Sox ace. In fact, the youngster looked pretty Crochet-like with a 2.64 ERA in the first half, despite relying much less on the strikeout to generate that success. However, as we race toward October, it's time to start thinking about the postseason rotation, and we could see Bennett as the odd man out. Since August 1, the youngster has made seven starts
item.content:encoded:
Jake Bennett might not be Garrett Crochet, but the 25-year-old rookie has done an admirable job this season filling in for the injured Boston Red Sox ace. In fact, the youngster looked pretty Crochet-like with a 2.64 ERA in the first half, despite relying much less on the strikeout to generate that success.
However, as we race toward October, it's time to start thinking about the postseason rotation, and we could see Bennett as the odd man out. Since August 1, the youngster has made seven starts and posted a 5.26 ERA.
The way he's performed over his last three starts has been interesting. On August 29, he twirled six scoreless innings against the New York Yankees while allowing just three hits. On September 3, he took the ball against the Baltimore Orioles and again went six deep, this time surrendering three runs. The two outings were basically the opposite ends of the spectrum of what we'd consider acceptable for a starter in the playoff rotation.
That Orioles start had a hidden concern, though. Bennett served up two homers, and it would prove prophetic for the next time he took the mound. That came on September 9 against the hapless Los Angeles Angels, who torched him for six earned runs over 5 1/3 innings. Bennett got taken deep three times in the affair and allowed eight balls to be hit over 100 miles per hour. His average exit velo for the start was a whopping 95.6 miles per hour.
At the same time, his chief competition for a spot in the playoff rotation, Ranger Suarez, might be rounding into form. The veteran struggled mightily in August after returning from the groin issue that landed him on the IL back in July, posting a 5.70 ERA for the month.
His lone start of September, though, was vintage Suarez, turning in seven shutout innings while allowing just five hits and a walk and generating a whole lot of soft contact.
If Ranger Suarez can prove he's back, he'll swipe Jake Bennett's spot in the Red Sox's playoff rotation
One start doesn't erase all the concern, but Suarez earned the second All-Star nod of his career thanks to his mostly stellar work in the first half. It's not unreasonable to assume that his string of uninspiring August performances was simply due to him knocking off the rust after being on the IL.
For Bennett, there's an added layer. With 105 innings already on his ledger in the majors and another 39 1/3 frames for the WooSox, he's well past what he's used to. In his first minor league season back in 2023, he pitched 63 frames. He missed the entire 2024 season after undergoing Tommy John surgery, and then came back to throw 75 1/3 innings last season.
Essentially, his 144 1/3 combined innings this year alone are greater than the 138 1/3 inning workload he's carried the last three years combined. He can say that the increased run hasn't affected him, but if the results on the field tell a different story, then that's the likely case.
There are two other factors to consider in the event of a proverbial tie. One, the Red Sox gave Suarez $130 million over the winter for a reason. Contracts shouldn't give an underperforming player a boost over a younger, cheaper option, but if all else is equal, it can help to be the deciding factor.
More importantly, Suarez is experienced in October. During his time with the Phillies, he's thrown 42 2/3 playoff innings and owns a 1.48 postseason ERA. That experience, and more importantly, excellence, matters, especially when it seems that the other option is running out of gas.

item.title: [The New York Times] Trevor Story, productive in return from surgery, has something to prove for Red Sox

item.content:encoded:
BOSTON — In a one-run game against the Kansas City Royals’ last homestand, Boston Red Sox shortstop Trevor Story hit a one-out double off the wall, raced to second base and dove head-first into the bag.
He flipped over on his back and held onto the bag, a safe call upheld after a Royals’ challenge.
Advertisement
The Red Sox eventually lost that game, but it was a small play that represented the bigger picture: Story was back. A diving, flipping play would have been hard to imagine for Story — or anyone watching him — earlier this season as he battled through a sports hernia injury that left him hitting .206 with a .547 OPS after 41 games.
Following surgery in May and a rehab that forced him to miss 93 games this season, Story has made a quiet but impactful return to the team.
He has hit safely in 13 of 14 games since returning, including Tuesday’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers. Since his activation Aug. 30 in New York, Story has started at shortstop in 14 of the team’s 15 games, going 19-for-56 (.339) with seven doubles and six RBIs. He’s hoping to make up for lost time.
“That was, ideally, the point of the surgery, to get it and come back and be able to do the things that I know I can do,” the 33-year-old said.
“It’s not invisible,” he said of the sports hernia’s effects. “I don’t think you would expect it to be after surgery and coming back. But it’s so much better than it was, and I’m getting stronger. So I’m happy about that. And I’m happy with the way my body has reacted. I wanted to be a part of this.”
It’s admittedly a small sample size since Story has returned, but if he had started slowly following his return, the calls for him to be replaced in the lineup would have grown louder. His replacements at shortstop — particularly a combination of Andruw Monasterio and Nick Sogard — filled in admirably during his absence as the Red Sox turned their season around. Story’s unproductive 10 rehab games with Triple-A Worcester, coupled with the rise of top prospect Franklin Arias, a shortstop raking at Triple A, created an echo chamber of angst about Story returning and underperforming.
So far, he hasn’t.
Advertisement
And he’s heard much of the criticism and frustration about his impending return. He understands it. His injury-riddled tenure in Boston has warranted that consternation. He missed much of 2024 recovering from extensive shoulder surgery and 2023 from elbow surgery. Of his five years in Boston, on a six-year, $140 million deal, he’s played only one healthy season.
Staying on the field has been his biggest bugaboo with the Red Sox. But the outside noise and frustration with his injuries motivated Story to prove he can still play.
“You see a lot of that stuff, but I really try to channel it into an energy in a way that I can use,” he said. “At the time, I wasn’t trying to pay much attention to it, but people would bring it to me, and I decided how I was going to look at it. I just tried to channel it into when I do come back, and it’s all about the playoffs, and it’s all about winning this thing at the end. That’s where I put my energy and focus.”
Roman Anthony, who missed 101 games with a torn finger ligament and rehabbed alongside Story, learned by watching the veteran handle the pressure.
“He’s unbelievable,” said Anthony. “Getting to go through this process with him. I was so happy for him. Every at-bat, he just continues to look better and better, and then to trust himself through all the noise.”
The return to the field has taken Story some effort, though. He arrives at the field roughly an hour before the team’s mandatory report time so that he can get on the trainer’s table to be stretched out for 30 to 45 minutes before his activation work in the gym, which leads into the team’s daily hitters’ meeting, then his workout before cage and field work.
“I’ve learned to kind of streamline it a little bit, and with the injury, (I) kind of know what (I) need,” he said. “In the gym, I’m just activating the right muscles, getting the core going, getting the hips right, adductor, glute med, the surrounding muscles from my surgery. So a lot of it is pre-hab. It’s mainly about the hips and getting the rotations right.”
Advertisement
The work has paid off early on. On Aug. 31, his first game back at Fenway Park in nearly four months, he cranked a base hit off the wall in the bottom of the ninth for a walk-off win.
This past Sunday, he padded a slim Red Sox lead against the Royals with a two-run single in the eighth. He’s hoping to carry this production through the rest of the season to prove he can be the player who hit .289 with an .827 OPS over the final four months of the 2025 season.
Despite missing so much of the year, the recent production since has helped him feel a part of the Red Sox’ run.
“As I’m sitting there watching the 15-game winning streak and starting to turn the whole season around, you watch it from the dugout and it’s like, ‘Man, this is something special,'” he said. “To be able to play a part and do my thing this late in the season means a lot to me.”

item.title: [Talk Sox] Jarren Duran Can Be Fixed, but the Red Sox Are Running Out of Time
item.dc:creator: N B Lindberg
item.description: Red Sox Video The Boston Red Sox are a near-lock for the second AL Wild Card spot. item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Video
The Boston Red Sox are a near-lock for the second AL Wild Card spot. With just over 10 games left in the season, it’d take a whole mess of crazy for the Sox to move up or down. While it would be great to have a shot at moving up in the standings, their current situation will allow them to spend the final two weeks of the season freshening up their stalwarts, getting injury returnees back up to speed, and fixing Jarren Duran.
Duran hasn’t quite been the worst regular in Major League Baseball, but that’s damning with faint praise. He’s still an excellent baserunner and a plus fielder, but only Ezequiel Tovar has a lower wRC+ (51) among qualified hitters than Duran’s mark of 67. Despite his disintegrated noodle of a bat, he has racked up 578 plate appearances due to injuries and, presumably, a lack of better options, but that doesn’t make him a lost cause.
What makes Duran’s complete collapse at the plate so shocking is that he was a top-25 hitter by wRC+ only two seasons ago (132), and well above average just last season (112). While it’s safe to assume 2024 was a career year, he looked to have established himself as an above-average bat, and it’s not like all of his underlying metrics have cratered. If anything, many have improved.
He’s swinging the bat as fast as ever. His barrel rate is almost identical to the past two seasons. He’s pulling the ball in the air more. And while his in-zone contact rate is a career-low 84%, that’s a completely fair trade-off for what should be better power.
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
Now, you could argue that Duran didn’t need to change his approach from 2024, but given these figures, there’d be no reason to believe he had gone from one of the best hitters in baseball to almost the very worst. However, this chart doesn’t contain every last kernel of underlying data, and the one thing that has cratered for Duran is the most basic, fundamental skill of hitting—not chasing (f***ing) fastballs out of the zone.
Duran is running a wRC+ of 67 because his out-of-zone swing rate (O-Swing%) has ballooned to 34.5%, which is largely driven by a career-high O-Swing% of 36.8% against four-seam fastballs. Throughout his career, Duran’s production has largely followed his ability to lay off pitches out of the zone, but his inability to lay off four-seam fastballs (FA), to this degree, is new.
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
What makes his cratering performance against four-seamers so baffling is that it is exclusively down to swing decisions. His production when he makes contact is relatively unchanged, and he’s not whiffing a concerning amount in the zone. In fact, his zone contact rate against four-seamers is better than it was in 2024.
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
It’s not groundbreaking analysis to say that swinging at fastballs out of the zone is a bad idea, but it doesn’t necessarily doom a hitter to the abyss. However, Duran’s ability against four-seamers was a load-bearing trait, and it becoming a weakness has completely collapsed his profile because it has cost him the platoon advantage.
Unsurprisingly, Duran, a left-handed hitter, has made a career out of pulverizing right-handed pitching. His career wRC+ against righties is 114, compared to 72 against lefties. Splits like this are far from unusual, but what has happened to Duran in 2026 is. Over 410 plate appearances against righties, he has a wRC+ of 63. That’s the second-worst among qualified hitters, and it all stems from his struggles against four-seam fastballs.
This season, 37.3% of the pitches right-handers have thrown Duran have been four-seam fastballs, right in line with his career average of 38.7%. While four-seamers generally have more neutral platoon splits, historically, Duran absolutely feasted on right-handed four-seamers. Entering 2026, Duran had a +20.6 run value against right-handed four-seam fastballs, but he has somehow managed an absolutely preposterous, incomprehensible -13.1 run value in 2026.
The reason why Duran’s plate discipline has completely collapsed against four-seamers is a bit more of a mystery, but I think it starts with his increased desire to swing hard, lift, and pull. Over the past four seasons, as Duran’s swing speed has increased, he has hit the ball out in front a bit more.
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
None of this is particularly surprising and should be expected. A faster bat will make contact out in front more often, and bat speed increases throughout a swing. The two moving in tandem make all the sense in the world, but getting to this point could have come at a cost.
To sell out for swing speed and contact out in front, Duran likely has to get his operation started just a fraction of a second earlier, which means committing to pitches a tad earlier as well. The trickle-down effect is swinging at more pitches out of the zone, and in particular four-seam fastballs, which require the quickest decisions at the plate.
The Red Sox don’t need Jarren Duran to figure it out to make the playoffs, but getting him back to basics could unlock another level of the offense. With Duran producing at an average offensive level, suddenly the Sox could field an elite outfield defense of Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, and Duran, while letting Roman Anthony DH. However, for that dream arrangement to work, Duran needs to actually hit again, and that starts with laying off fastballs outside of the zone.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] The Red Sox took great pains to build depth in the offseason, and the results are paying off - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Alex Speier
item.description: ARLINGTON, Texas — For the Red Sox, the vision of contention in 2026 seemed straightforward. The team’s championship window had been pried open by the presence of a pair of cornerstones, with Garrett Crochet anchoring the rotation and Roman Anthony representing a lineup anchor not only for this year but several seasons to come. item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — For the Red Sox, the vision of contention in 2026 seemed straightforward.
The team’s championship window had been pried open by the presence of a pair of cornerstones, with Garrett Crochet anchoring the rotation and Roman Anthony representing a lineup anchor not only for this year but several seasons to come.
But while the Sox are amid a magic-number countdown to a playoff berth, they’ve done so without Anthony and Crochet for most of the year. Their season has been saved in no small part by players who have emerged from obscurity to play critical roles — with essential contributions coming from Andruw Monasterio, Anthony Seigler, Mickey Gasper, Tsung-Che Cheng, Jahmai Jones, Tyron Guerrero, and more.
“I don’t think anybody had that on the drawing board,” said interim manager Chad Tracy with a chuckle. “They were asked to play a lot, and they produced. And if they didn’t, we were in trouble. It’s a huge piece of the 2026 season, no question.”
Of course, while no one expected the outsized impact of players who began the year as big league backups or in Triple-A, the Sox also took considerable pains to build organizational depth through a variety of transactions.
Whether it was an expanded version of the trade that brought Caleb Durbin from Milwaukee to include Monasterio and Seigler, or waiver claims of Cheng and Gasper, or a minor league deal for Guerrero, the season has been a case study in the notion that perceived little moves can have a huge impact.
“Every move and every decision matters,” said assistant general manager Mike Groopman, who oversees the team’s acquisitions group. “The big ones, whether it’s a larger free agent deal, [or] a larger, more high-profile trade, is naturally going to get a lot of attention.
“I don’t think this is unique to the Red Sox. There are 29 other teams that try to and do a very good job about caring about the ‘little’ things. But I think what we really try to reinforce is … that year over year, around the game, you see things that seem ‘little’ that end up being really impactful and big. [Deals that] seemed like small moves at the outset end up having a much, much larger impact commensurate with what would have been perceived at the time as a ‘larger’ move.”
Players who evolve from theoretical depth to become big league contributors excite numerous corners of an organization. The primary credit for those contributions, of course, belongs with a player, but they still often represent the combined efforts of personnel in scouting who identify the player’s potential contributions, player development personnel who help the player build on preexisting strengths and abilities in the minors, and big league staffers who help the players to perform at the game’s highest level.
Take Guerrero. After brief stints in the big leagues in 2018 and 2019, he’d become a journeyman, shuffling between organizations — and countries — but unable to forge a way back to the big leagues despite elite velocity.
But the Sox — who’d been interested in signing Guerrero before he pitched in the NPB in Japan in 2025 — remained intrigued, thanks in part to strong scouting recommendations from Kento Matsumoto in Japan and Manny Nanita in the Dominican Winter League. After they signed Guerrero to a minor league deal in the offseason, player development officials worked with him on some minor grip changes that unlocked significantly improved command with a sinker that regularly reached triple digits.
Guerrero’s dominance this year in Triple-A (0.92 ERA) essentially forced the Sox to call him up, and the 35-year-old emerged as a late-innings force from late June to late August (before shoulder fatigue led to a bad outing followed by a trip to the injured list), posting a 2.13 ERA over a 23-appearance stretch.
Again, the lion’s share of the credit goes to Guerrero for the work he did to fight his way back to the big leagues. But his emergence embodies the sort of under-the-radar acquisition that helped save the Sox’ season.
“The connection and integration between acquisition and development is really important,” said Groopman. “Guerrero and our [player development] group put a lot of time into [those changes] in the spring and the early season, to get him to a point where he was able to lock in some of these changes and unlock what was super obvious arm talent into something that was translating more consistently onto the major league mound.”
Of course, talent alone doesn’t dictate success once a depth player gets to the big leagues. They must also have the opportunity to contribute — and, in many cases, the freedom to fail while getting their bearings.
Tracy, who spent time with nearly all of this year’s depth contributors in Triple-A at the beginning of the year, has been mindful of creating an environment in which call-ups can contribute.
“I’m in the same boat [as them]. I want the freedom to go manage the game [as a first-time big league manager],” said Tracy. “I need to manage a game and feel like if I do something that doesn’t go right, it’s not the end of the world. If I feel that way, then I want the player to feel like, ‘Hey, if you go out there and play second base today and you make an error, move on to the next play.’
“If the culture becomes, ‘If I make a mistake, then all of a sudden I clam up and I get really tight,’ we’re going to have a problem. So you look at them and say, ‘You’re here for a reason: To go play your game. Don’t worry about making a mistake. Move on to the next pitch, next play.’ And they did that, and they were awesome.”
Alex Speier can be reached at alex.speier@globe.com. Follow him @alexspeier.
