item.content:encoded:
Heading into the playoffs, the Boston Red Sox have one of the best bullpens in all of baseball. A major reason why is the dominance of setup man Garrett Whitlock.
At one point, Whitlock was a pitcher who the Red Sox had hoped to make into a starter. His body, seemingly, couldn’t handle the workload, though. So, he moved to the bullpen where he’s been dominant. Still, there is a willingness that Whitlock recently shared with The Boston Globe to return to the rotation.
“I definitely know my body better and know everything better now, and so it’s definitely something I’d be open to. Will I?” Whitlock said. “I’m not going to walk into [chief baseball officer Craig Breslow’s] office and be like, ‘Hey, I’m starting.’ So it’s one of those things where the team would have to be on board with it and just talk through everything and go through it. But it’s something I’d always be open to.”
It’s been since 2024 when Whitlock last started for the Red Sox. Since then, he’s become one of the game’s elite relievers. In 2026 alone, he has a 1.81 ERA, a 0.826 WHIP, and 10.5 strikeouts per nine in 49.2 innings of work.
“I doubt Boston will do it. We’re pretty good on starting depth,” Whitlock said. “If I become a free agent and a team approaches me about it, I’m open to it and see how it goes.”
Whitlock is a different pitcher now than he was when he was starting games. He’s a sinker pitcher now, and he’s ditched his fastball. He’s also changed his changeup grip, making it one of the best pitches in MLB.
Seth Lugo of the Kansas City Royals recently made a similar switch back and forth. As he explained it, the switch back to starting is actually easier.
“Once you make the switch back, you have the confidence. The problems you had earlier in your career, [which] sent you to the ’pen in the first place — you’re aware why those mistakes happened,” Lugo said.
Injuries Have Plagued Garrett Whitlock With the Boston Red Sox
The major reason why the Red Sox sent Garrett Whitlock to the bullpen was that his body wasn’t holding up to the workload. Injuries became a major issue at that point in his career.
Among the injuries Whitlock has battled in his career are a right pec strain, right hip inflammation, right hip impingement, right elbow ulnar neuritis, right elbow inflammation again, and in 2024 he would finally need an internal brace to repair a torn UCL. It was an alternative to Tommy John. Even in 2026, as a reliever, Whitlock landed on the IL with a left leg strain.
Still, he’s stayed healthier in the bullpen overall. So, it’s made sense to keep him there.
Whitlock isn’t the only starter forced into the bullpen over the years. He’s even fairly close with a couple of them from his time on Team USA in the World Baseball Classic. They’re even able to joke about that role now.
“We all joke that we’re all failed starters,” Whitlock said.
Whitlock’s Contract Situation With the Red Sox
In April of 2022, the Red Sox extended Garrett Whitlock. He’s currently on a four-year, $18.75 million deal. That’s going to expire at the end of the season, though there are club options for the next two seasons.
When the Red Sox signed that extension, Whitlock was a starting pitcher. Now a relief pitcher, the value of the deal does change a little bit. His 2027 option is worth $8.25 million and the 2028 option is worth $10.5 million.
The Red Sox certainly don’t want to see Whitlock walk. The 30 year old has, undeniably, been elite for them. So, they are going to need to consider their options. That is, to pick up those options, extend Whitlock again, or let him walk in free agency. Making that a tougher decision are the upcoming CBA negotiations.
Notably, even Whitlock’s 2028 option would be outside the current top 10 in AAV for the 2026 season among relievers. So, for his production, the Red Sox are getting great value.

item.title: [WHDH] Roman Anthony, Red Sox fans praise pitcher Payton Tolle after immaculate inning: ‘He’s amazing’ - Boston News, Weather, Sports | WHDH 7News
item.dc:creator: Maria D'Agostino

item.content:encoded:
BOSTON (WHDH) - Red Sox rookie Payton Tolle Sunday became just the sixth pitcher in MLB history to throw an immaculate inning in the first inning of a game. An immaculate inning occurs when a pitcher records three strikeouts on nine pitches.
The 23-year-old lefty has quickly become a fan favorite through not only his pitching prowess, but by showcasing his infectious personality. On the eighth pitch of the inning, Tolle flashed a bright smile into the Red Sox dugout before getting Kansas City Royals right fielder Jac Caglianone to strikeout swinging, completing the rare feat.
“We saw him smile towards the end and…said ‘oh my gosh it’s almost immaculate inning,’ and then he got it. And we were just floored,” said Caroline Stacey, a Red Sox fan from Maine. “Tolle is such a great player, he’s so fun to watch. Like, everything he does is just fun so it was really great to see him celebrate and have such an amazing accomplishment.”
The last Red Sox player to throw an immaculate inning at the start of a game was Hall-of-Famer Pedro Martinez in 2002. The then-30-year-old struck out three Mariners in a row on May 18.
“Unbelievable. Eighth in the history of the Red Sox is, I mean, unbelievable,” said Chris Molina, a Red Sox fan visiting Boston from Kansas.
After the game, Tolle said he hopes to ignite the team in any way he can.
“Trying to be the spark in whatever way I can. If that’s pitching or that’s offense, just trying to find that way is kind of what I want to do,” he explained.
It’s that spark that has him winning over the city of Boston as well as his teammates. Red Sox star outfielder Roman Anthony praised Tolle during an on field interview after the game on NESN.
“You see the amount of people that are behind him, and the energy he brings to Red Sox baseball and the city of Boston,” Anthony said. “Everyone around, they ride for him, and we feel that energy when he’s on the bump the minute he takes it. He’s such an amazing person, and an amazing teammate who’s there for us every single day, and whether he’s pitching or not he brings that energy. So it’s so fun to be behind him. He’s amazing.”
The manager of the Red Sox Team Store says they can barely keep his jersey stocked on the shelves as the demand has become so high.
“When you combine the talent that he has with the personality that he has – we’ve seen this before with certain guys like Johnny Damon, David Ortiz, who were big personalities and great players – I mean, that means he’s going to be a star for years to come,” said Tim Pettit, Manager of the Red Sox Team Store.
Following the immaculate inning, Tolle went on to throw five more scoreless innings, finishing with seven strikeouts. The Red Sox went on to beat the Royals 4-1 and secure the series win.

item.title: [The Portland Press Herald] Payton Tolle 1st Red Sox pitcher since Pedro Martinez in 2002 to start game with immaculate inning
item.dc:creator: Ken Powtak; Scott Martin
item.description: BOSTON — Boston Red Sox left-hander Payton Tolle pitched an immaculate inning to open Sunday’s game against the Kansas City Royals. The 23-year-old left-hander threw a called third strike past Nick Loftin, then got Bobby Witt Jr. and Jac Caglianone swinging in the nine-pitch inning. Tolle became Boston’s first pitcher to throw an immaculate inning opening a game since Hall of Famer Pedro Martinez at Fenway Park against Seattle on May 18, 2002. “It was pretty cool. It was a pretty cool feeling,”
item.content:encoded:
BOSTON — Boston Red Sox left-hander Payton Tolle pitched an immaculate inning to open Sunday’s game against the Kansas City Royals.
The 23-year-old left-hander threw a called third strike past Nick Loftin, then got Bobby Witt Jr. and Jac Caglianone swinging in the nine-pitch inning.
Tolle became Boston’s first pitcher to throw an immaculate inning opening a game since Hall of Famer Pedro Martinez at Fenway Park against Seattle on May 18, 2002.
“It was pretty cool. It was a pretty cool feeling,” Tolle said after the Red Sox beat the Royals 4-1 to win the series. “That was the first time, I think in high school I might have had a couple of opportunities at it. That was fun, that was cool.”
Caglianone was the only one to get his bat on a ball, fouling his first pitch to the left side.
When Tolle got two strikes on Caglianone, most of the fans rose and cheered loudly. Tolle pumped a fist when the strikeout and inning were complete after looking over at the dugout with a bit of a smile before the last pitch.
“I was definitely thinking about it,” he said. “I looked over at (pitching coach Andrew Bailey) and he was smiling, too.”
It was Boston’s eighth immaculate inning, the second in the first inning and the sixth in MLB recorded history to open the game. Hall of Famer Sandy Koufax had the first recorded one on June 30, 1962.
Chris Sale had the most recent for the Red Sox on Aug. 26, 2021, at Fenway against Minnesota.
Tolle went six scoreless innings with seven strikeouts and allowed four singles.

item.title: [elplaneta.com] Inning inmaculado: la histórica gesta de Payton Tolle en Fenway Park
item.dc:creator: Marcos Grunfeld
item.description: Los Red Sox tuvieron que retrasar dos veces el inicio del juego del domingo debido a la lluvia que azotó Boston en el cierre de la semana. item.content:encoded:
Los Red Sox tuvieron que retrasar dos veces el inicio del juego del domingo debido a la lluvia que azotó Boston en el cierre de la semana. Fue imposible jugar antes de las 4:55 de la tarde, casi cuatro horas después de lo inicialmente estipulado porque iba a ser un domingo normal con el primer pitcheo lanzándose a la 1:35 de la tarde.
En la medida que se acercaban las 3:00 p.m iba despejándose la duda de que tampoco a esa hora iba a iniciar el duelo entre los patirojos y los Reales de Kansas City. En todo caso, el pitcher Payton Tolle se acercó a su manager Chad Tracy, le hizo un saludo militar y le dijo que estaría listo a la hora que el partido comenzara.
El zurdo no estaba mintiendo. A las 4:55 p.m tiró una recta de 95 millas en strike. Ocho envíos después consiguió una hazaña que solo ocho miembros del club habían conseguido. El monticulista tiró ocho rectas y un sinker para ponchar a sus tres primeros rivales con nueve strikes en fila y convertirse en el octavo miembro de la franquicia en lograr un inning inmaculado.
Es el segundo que lo consigue en el primer inning uniéndose al legendario Pedro Martínez.
“Fue divertido”, celebró Tolle después de la victoria de 4 a 1. “Fue chévere. Creo que después del tercer strike me vino la idea a la cabeza. Pero eso no debería pasar. Creo que debería ser mejor y no andar pensando en esas cosas, pero así sucedió”.
La transmisión del equipo captó el momento previo al último envío antes de la hazaña. Tolle miró a su dugout y sonrió. Dio cuenta que estaba al tanto de lo estaba por suceder en conchupancia con su coach de pitcheo Andrew Bailey.
“Estaba definitivamente pensando en eso”, contó. “Lo tenía en mente. Creo que miré a “Bales” y estaba sonriendo también. Fue divertido”.
Solo ocho monticulistas de los Red Sox habían conseguido esa gesta. El último había sido Chris Sale en mayo de 2021.
“Fue impresionante”, agregó el primera base Willson Contreras, quien regresó a la acción después de casi dos semanas lesionado. “Estuvo atacando la zona de strike. No estaba permitiendo mucha gente en base. Creo que es la primera vez que soy parte de algo así”.
Payton Tolle siguió brillando después de la hazaña y terminó con seis innings completos, sin permitir carreras, un bateador golpeado, cuatro hits y siete ponches.
Y si les quedó alguna duda sobre el saludo militar, tal parece es una broma que se gasta con Tracy todos los días.
“Tiene haciéndolo desde que llegué acá”, bromeó Tracy. “No le pedí que lo hiciera. Solo lo hace. No necesito que lo haga, pero es Tolle y eso es lo que hace”.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Masataka Yoshida’s potential return creates another complicated Red Sox roster decision
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello
item.description: The Boston Red Sox never fully resolved their outfield-designated hitter logjam, and once again it may create a roster conundrum. For much of the season, things had worked themselves out one way or another. Spending most of the season without Roman Anthony certainly wasn't ideal, but it did make for a cleaner lineup card. His return, of course, has been music to our ears, and it saved the Red Sox from another tough roster decision due to the injuries to Masataka Yoshida and Ceddanne Rafaela. The
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox never fully resolved their outfield-designated hitter logjam, and once again it may create a roster conundrum. For much of the season, things had worked themselves out one way or another.
Spending most of the season without Roman Anthony certainly wasn't ideal, but it did make for a cleaner lineup card. His return, of course, has been music to our ears, and it saved the Red Sox from another tough roster decision due to the injuries to Masataka Yoshida and Ceddanne Rafaela.
There's a point where push might come to shove, though, and Boston is forced to make a tough choice. Chad Tracy won't rule out Yoshida returning in time for the playoffs, which would lead to some interesting decisions.
"He's [Yoshida] not on the 60-day (injured list). It's just a matter of how does he heal over the next handful of weeks," the interim skipper said.
If the 33-year-old can return in time for October, it could put the likes of Mickey Gasper or Nick Sogard in the crosshairs. At which point, the Red Sox will have to make a choice and leave someone unhappy.
Masataka Yoshida shouldn't cost Mickey Gasper or Nick Sogard a spot on the Red Sox playoff roster
Just because Yoshida can come back (and that's still up in the air) doesn't mean he should. The NPB veteran has done what he's always done since coming stateside, hit for some average and get on base, but has provided very little in the power department.
Through 87 games, he's hit .274/.347/.399 with five homers, which is nothing to sneeze at, but doesn't really scratch the Red Sox's power itch. On top of that, despite what we saw in the World Baseball Classic, he has little defensive value and will be a nonfactor in the outfield coming off a serious hamstring strain.
Comparatively, Gasper's hot bat better fits what Boston needs. While he might simply be riding the wave rather than emerging as a true offensive force, the switch-hitter has brought the pop with eight dingers in just 187 plate appearances and a .500 slugging percentage, all while providing similar contact and on-base numbers to Yoshida.
Furthermore, he has some value in the field with the ability to fill in behind the plate if needed, as well as play first base. That alone gives him an edge over the DH-only Yoshida.
As for Sogard, his offensive profile is similar to Yoshida's, but his positional versatility is far superior. Depending on Curtis Mead's recovery, Sogard is a valuable insurance policy at second base that should have him over Yoshida in the October pecking order, too.
Craig Breslow's failure to move Jarren Duran before he became a radioactive asset is the real key here. Not only does it represent a missed opportunity for the Red Sox, but it is also the main barrier for Yoshida, given that Boston can't really afford to carry a DH-only player. With that, the choice should be clear. Even if Yoshida is healthy, he needs to sit this October out.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Deep down, Garrett Whitlock doesn’t think his career as a starting pitcher is over - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tim Healey
item.description: Now is not the time, of course, what with the Red Sox in a playoff push and all. But deep down inside, in a maybe-one-day-eventually sort of way, Garrett Whitlock harbors aspirations to try again to be a starting pitcher, to return to the rotation. Consider it a curiosity. “I definitely know my body better and know everything better now, and so it’s definitely something I’d be open to. Will I?” Whitlock said. “I’m not going to walk into [chief baseball officer Craig Breslow’s] office and be like
item.content:encoded:
Now is not the time, of course, what with the Red Sox in a playoff push and all.
But deep down inside, in a maybe-one-day-eventually sort of way, Garrett Whitlock harbors aspirations to try again to be a starting pitcher, to return to the rotation.
Consider it a curiosity.
“I definitely know my body better and know everything better now, and so it’s definitely something I’d be open to. Will I?” Whitlock said. “I’m not going to walk into [chief baseball officer Craig Breslow’s] office and be like, ‘Hey, I’m starting.’ So it’s one of those things where the team would have to be on board with it and just talk through everything and go through it. But it’s something I’d always be open to.”
Whitlock is intrigued enough to have picked the brain in recent months of Griffin Jax, the righthander whom the Rays converted from reliever to starter this season.
Jax, 31, had an 8.00 ERA in 11 relief appearances, moved to the rotation in April, slowly built up his pitch count, and has a 3.59 ERA in 20 starts.
Whitlock and Jax became buddies when they played together for Team USA during the World Baseball Classic in March. They’ve texted about what amounts to an experiment for Jax.
Jax’s take, per Whitlock: Everything he learned in his years as a reliever, several as a high-end reliever, made him a better pitcher, regardless of role. Tweaks to his repertoire, knowing how to attack hitters, and ensuring his body recovers between outings — it all applies to being a starter.
Whitlock has had similar conversations with the Cubs’ Clay Holmes, another Team USA teammate. He made the switch last year.
“We all joke that we’re all failed starters,” Whitlock said of his bullpen brethren.
Take it from the Royals’ Seth Lugo, who beat the Red Sox on Friday.
He and Whitlock have had very similar career arcs: They reached the majors in their mid-20s as non-elite prospects, bounced between the bullpen and rotation based on team need and their performance, and accepted their club wanting them in a relief role. They were excellent at it.
All along, Lugo, a consummate pro and good employee in his years as a Mets reliever, said he wanted to give starting another go — someday. Now, he is in his fourth season and third contract since getting the chance — once he became a free agent — and turning it into a successful and lucrative second act.
“It’s not as daunting as it seems,” Lugo said at Fenway Park over the weekend. “What happens is you first get to the big leagues and you try to be someone that you’re not, just from other influences, other recommendations. But you [learn] how to get guys out [as a reliever].
“Once you make the switch back, you have the confidence. The problems you had earlier in your career, [which] sent you to the ’pen in the first place — you’re aware why those mistakes happened.”
Lugo, like Whitlock, was a late-innings arm. He faced the other team’s best hitters in some of the most important moments of the game.
“Once you have success pitching the seventh, eighth, ninth inning, the first six innings become a lot easier,” he said. “As a reliever, when you’re going into a game, you’re a lot more stressed out than you are as a starter. So you start to recognize what you’re good at, how you can get out of those situations.”
Whitlock, who possesses a 1.81 ERA in 51 relief appearances this year, last made more than a handful of starts in 2023. Since then, he ditched the four-seam fastball to lean even more on his sinker, went with a slider instead of a sweeper, and changed his changeup, which has become highly effective.
In discussing the possibility, Whitlock is a realist: The Sox’ rotation seems full for the foreseeable future.
His contract includes team options for 2027 ($8.25 million) and 2028 ($10.5 million). Those are good deals for an elite reliever — and a really good deal for even a serviceable starter.
“I doubt Boston will do it. We’re pretty good on starting depth,” Whitlock said. “If I become a free agent and a team approaches me about it, I’m open to it and see how it goes.”
Perez on Abreu
Royals icon and Venezuela captain Salvador Perez, witness to Wilyer Abreu’s WBC star turn, is a big fan — and a big believer of Abreu on a big stage. “He’s going to be the MVP if Boston makes it to the World Series,” Perez said. “He’s built for a moment like that.” … Early returns on Adley Rutschman’s cortisone shot last week, intended to alleviate pain in his right elbow, are solid. Against Kansas City, he went 3 for 10 with a double, as many walks as strikeouts (two) — and played three games in a row for the first time since getting hurt. “It definitely helped a lot,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “You can tell his body language and stuff too, he looks and feels pretty good.” … Garrett Crochet’s bullpen session Tuesday is scheduled for 30 pitches across two simulated innings, a step up from previous shorter sessions.
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Old teammate Kurt Suzuki has only positive words for Craig Breslow and Andrew Bailey, and other Red Sox thoughts - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Peter Abraham
item.description: Andrew Bailey, Craig Breslow, and Kurt Suzuki were teammates with the Oakland Athletics from 2009-11. Now Bailey is the Red Sox pitching coach, Breslow is chief baseball officer, and Suzuki is managing the Angels. Suzuki, a former catcher, knows the Red Sox pitching coach and chief baseball officer well. Bailey was a two-time All-Star closer with the Athletics, and Breslow made 202 appearances as a setup man during that time. “I thought Bres would cure cancer when he was finished with baseball,”
item.content:encoded:
Andrew Bailey, Craig Breslow, and Kurt Suzuki were teammates with the Oakland Athletics from 2009-11. Now Bailey is the Red Sox pitching coach, Breslow is chief baseball officer, and Suzuki is managing the Angels.
Suzuki, a former catcher, knows the Red Sox pitching coach and chief baseball officer well. Bailey was a two-time All-Star closer with the Athletics, and Breslow made 202 appearances as a setup man during that time.
“I thought Bres would cure cancer when he was finished with baseball,” said Suzuki, referencing the lefthander graduating from Yale with a degree in molecular biophysics and biochemistry. “But I can see why he stayed in baseball. He was always ahead of the times the way he thought about the game.
“When I caught him, I called him ‘Everyday Bres.’ He was always ready to pitch every day, never complained, and always got people out. He was a good person to be around.”
Suzuki is not surprised to see his former teammates still involved in the game.
“I think we all love the game. We all had an interest to stay in the game beyond our playing time,” he said. “Bres pitched in the big leagues for a long time and gained a lot of information. I don’t know if I would have predicted he’d be running a team, but I’m not surprised.
“The same with [Bailey]. You knew he would have a bright future in the game if that was what he wanted. He’s one of the best pitching coaches around.”
A few other observations on the Red Sox:
▪ It seems funny to think about now, but Aroldis Chapman came to spring training in 2025 with no guarantee he would be the closer.
The lefthander was competing with Liam Hendriks, who was returning from Tommy John surgery. Breslow said at the time Justin Slaten also would receive consideration.
Chapman had 14 saves for the Pirates in 2024, but nine of them came in September for a last-place team.
Hendriks never had a save for the Sox. Slaten had one in March and two in April that season, and none since.
Chapman has converted 65 of 69 save opportunities for the Sox and taken steps that could lead to the Hall of Fame.
▪ No Red Sox infielder has won a Gold Glove since Ian Kinsler in 2018, and he joined the team at the trade deadline that season and started only 35 games at second base. For a full season, you have to go back to Pedroia in 2014.
Caleb Durbin is set to break that drought.
The third baseman has 11 defensive runs saved, the most in the American League by a wide margin. Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero, with three, is a distant second. Durbin also leads in other metrics, including outs above average.
▪ As the season winds down, Wilyer Abreu is first in doubles, second in runs and home runs, fourth in RBIs, and fifth in OPS among AL outfielders.
The right fielder believes playing in the World Baseball Classic contributed significantly to that success.
“I worked a lot in the offseason to be prepared for the WBC,” Abreu said. “So when the season started, I was ready to go. That helped me a lot.”
Abreu also benefited from being around Venezuela hitting coach Miguel Cabrera and assistant manager Victor Martinez.
“I talked a lot to them about my approach and how to attack pitchers on what they throw,” he said. “Miggy was such a smart hitter, and he really helped me.”
▪ Fred Lynn was at Fenway Park for the Angels series this past week. He follows the Sox closely and often arrives at the park early to watch batting practice.
Most of the players had no idea who the 74-year-old guy with the good tan was, but Roman Anthony did and had a conversation on the field with Lynn on Tuesday.
“He was somebody I’d wanted to meet for a while, obviously. A legend,” Anthony said. “Somebody said he was out there, so I immediately wanted to say hello to him and his wife, and they were great.
“He shared some of his experiences here, his experiences when he left here. It was great to hear it.”
No. 19 talking to No. 19 was interesting to watch from a distance. Anthony received a lot of attention when he was called up last year, but nothing like the mania for Lynn and Jim Rice in 1975.
Anthony has looked up the statistics. He gets it.
“I got familiar with him when I got 19 when I first came up last year,” he said. “He was pretty excited about it and sent some love. Obviously, he was an unbelievable player, an unbelievable Red Sox. But a great human, too. It was awesome to interact with him.”
▪ The Sox traded for Curtis Mead on July 26. He started at second base against the Athletics in Sacramento the next day, and broke his left wrist when he was hit by a pitch in his second plate appearance.
Red Sox second basemen have since hit .245 with a .718 OPS and 21 RBIs. It’s not great, but nine American League teams have a lower OPS from their second basemen in that span, and 10 have a lower wRC+.
As for Mead, he is playing catch but isn’t hitting yet. The Sox haven’t ruled him out for the rest of the season, but interim manager Chad Tracy has acknowledged it’s unlikely Mead will return until 2027.
Connelly Early, who was traded for Mead, has yet to pitch for the Nationals because of an elbow injury. He is scheduled to make a rehab start for Double-A Harrisburg on Sunday. The Nationals hope he’ll be able to get into a major league game before the season ends.
▪ Baseball lost a legend last week when Joe McDonald passed away at the age of 97.
McDonald started in baseball in the 1940s working with the ticket takers at Ebbets Field. He joined the Mets in 1962 and became their general manager from 1975-80.
He later became GM of the Cardinals (1982-84) and Tigers (1991-92) before scouting for the Angels and Rockies. He finished his career scouting for the Red Sox from 2004-19.
“Joe was a joy to work with and always very generous in sharing his experience and expertise. He loved the game, was willing to go scout a player anywhere at any time, and just wanted to contribute,” said former Sox GM and current Fenway Sports Group senior adviser Theo Epstein, who hired McDonald. “Having two great former GMs like Joe and Bill Lajoie around was incredibly valuable to me. He will be missed.”
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.title: [NESN] Healthy Tanner Houck Hopes to Be a Difference Maker for Red Sox in Playoffs | NESN
item.dc:creator: Daniel Yanofsky
item.description: Tanner Houck started his career with plenty of hype, acting as someone who can do anything if given the opportunity. item.content:encoded:
Tanner Houck started his career with plenty of hype, acting as someone who can do anything if given the opportunity. Coming off an injury that kept him out of action throughout he 2026 season, he hopes the Red Sox could use him come playoff time.
The 24th overall pick in the 2017 MLB Draft, Houck was picked up as a starting pitcher. A chameleon, he adapted to any situation, acting as a starter, reliever, and closer. In 2022, he appeared in 32 games and was as durable as one could be.
Houck has shown flashes of brilliance but hasn’t found consistency. This year, he has been rehabbing after undergoing a special surgery of his ulnar collateral ligament. It’s a "hybrid reconstruction" with a flexor tendon repair.
That was last August. This year, the Red Sox, with high expectations, struggled at first. Now, they are playoff contenders, and Houck wouldn’t mind adding to the fun. That includes rejoining the team before the season ended.
"I had my mind set on one goal, going out there and just helping this team this year," Houck said via The Boston Globe. "I just truly believed that I could do it."
The recovery process was expected to be 12-14 months. However, Houck recently appeared in minor league rehab game and is scheduled to pitch for Triple-A Worcester on Tuesday and Saturday. His determination to compete comes at an interesting time.
As of September 14, the Red Sox are 8.5 games behind the Rays in the AL East. They own the second Wild Card spot with just a few weeks to go in the regular season. Catching the Yankees, on top of the Wild Card, would be ideal.
Houck is one of a few Red Sox members to experience playoff baseball at Fenway Park. If he’s cleared, it doesn’t matter the role given, Houck hopes he can just make a difference.
"Three innings out of the pen is a little bit more appealing than just being a one-inning limited-pitch-count guy," Houck said. "So if I can get built up for 40-50 pitches and help out in any way, then it’s a lot easier role. Any role that I can step in and go out there and help this team win, I’m in."

item.content:encoded:
Tolle mimics Pedro in immaculate first inning ... with more smiles
This browser does not support the video element.
This story was excerpted from Ian Browne’s Red Sox Beat newsletter. To read the full newsletter, click here. And subscribe to get it regularly in your inbox.
BOSTON – It was more than 24 years ago, and I was in my first year covering the Red Sox for MLB.com, and everyone in the press box, the stands and even the two dugouts at Fenway Park were feeling a little restless. That’s what happens when you sit through a two-hour and five-minute rain delay waiting for the game to start.
But Pedro Martínez had a way of making everything worth the wait.
So when Payton Tolle threw his immaculate first inning on Sunday – after a rain delay of nearly two hours – my mind immediately flashed back to May 18, 2002.
Feats like this, these rare milestone moments, are what set baseball apart.
I’ve seen two no-hitters, plus at least four cycles I remember off the top of my head, and countless other unforgettable moments.
The one thing I’ve still never seen live is a perfect game. Here’s hoping I’ll get to witness that someday.
Though I had a scheduled day off on Sunday and wasn’t in my press box perch to witness Tolle becoming the sixth Red Sox pitcher in history to throw an immaculate inning, I immediately flashed back to Martínez against the Mariners on that soggy Saturday nearly a quarter century ago.
Of the eight times on record that Red Sox pitchers have thrown immaculate innings (including three times by Chris Sale), Tolle and Martínez are the only two who started a game by doing so.
Martínez’s day started with the ultimate challenge – facing Ichiro Suzuki. The Seattle hit king was in just his second year stateside, but already a legend.
But he wasn’t ready for Martínez’s first two pitches – a pair of high fastballs which both went for called strikes. The third pitch was a changeup that Suzuki weakly waved through. Seldom had he looked so overmatched on a swing before or after that.
Mark McLemore was up next, and swung through a first-pitch curveball. Then he fouled off a fastball. And looked at a fastball on the outside corner to become Martínez’s second victim.
Ruben Sierra was all that stood between Martínez and what wound up being the only immaculate inning of his Hall of Fame career. Sierra watched a cutter go by for a strike, and looked at a fastball next to make it 0-2.
This browser does not support the video element.
At this point, the Fenway Park crowd stood as one.
“The crowd is standing already, in the first inning,” Red Sox radio play-by-play man Joe Castiglione, a sound of surprise in his voice, informed his audience.
When Martínez got Sierra to fish for a high fastball, the roar was instantaneous.
“That gave us a huge lift,” Boston’s Brian Daubach said after the game. “Running in from left field after the inning, I was like, 'All right, now we’ve got a game.’”
The Red Sox went on to win, 4-1, as Martinez improved to 10-0 against the Mariners with a 0.94 ERA covering 77 innings. Keep in mind that the Mariners of the late 90s and early 2000s were one of the best teams in the game.
While Tolle didn’t face that stiff of an opponent in the Royals, he did go through one of the best players in the game in Bobby Witt Jr. to accomplish his feat. Kansas City’s No. 2 hitter, Witt waved through three straight fastballs between 97 and 98 mph as the second punchout of the first inning.
One of the indelible moments from Tolle’s immaculate frames: the huge grin that spread across his face almost unconsciously between pitches eight and nine. He knew what he was on the verge of doing and soaked in the moment.
Martínez? He never smiled on the mound. He couldn’t compete and have fun at the same time, like Tolle has the unique ability to do.
As different as their personalities are, they are now forever linked in Red Sox history.

item.content:encoded:
We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.

item.content:encoded:
El lanzador zurdo de los Boston Red Sox, Payton Tolle, logró una entrada inmaculada para abrir el partido del domingo contra los Kansas City Royals.
El zurdo de 23 años ponchó a Nick Loftin con un tercer strike cantado y luego retiró a Bobby Witt Jr. y a Jac Caglianone por la vía del strikeout tirándole, todo ello en una entrada de nueve lanzamientos.
Tolle se convirtió en el primer lanzador de Boston en lograr una entrada inmaculada al inicio de un partido desde que lo hiciera el miembro del Salón de la Fama Pedro Martínez en Fenway Park contra Seattle, el 18 de mayo de 2002.
"Fue genial. Fue una sensación increíble", dijo Tolle después de que los Red Sox vencieran a los Royals 4-1 para llevarse la serie. "Fue la primera vez; creo que tal vez tuve un par de oportunidades de lograrlo en la secundaria. Fue divertido, fue genial".
Caglianone fue el único que logró hacer contacto con la pelota, enviando su primer lanzamiento de foul hacia el lado izquierdo.
Cuando Tolle acumuló dos strikes contra Caglianone, la mayoría de los aficionados se puso de pie y vitoreó con fuerza. Tolle celebró con un gesto de puño en alto al concretarse el ponche y finalizar la entrada, tras haber mirado hacia el dugout con una leve sonrisa antes del último lanzamiento.
"Definitivamente estaba pensando en ello", comentó. "Miré hacia donde estaba (el entrenador de lanzadores Andrew Bailey) y él también sonreía".
Fue la octava entrada inmaculada en la historia de Boston, la segunda lograda en el primer episodio y la sexta registrada en la historia de la MLB al inicio de un partido. Sandy Koufax, miembro del Salón de la Fama, protagonizó la primera registrada el 30 de junio de 1962.
Chris Sale había logrado la más reciente para los Red Sox el 26 de agosto de 2021, en Fenway Park y frente a Minnesota.
Tolle lanzó seis entradas en blanco, ponchó a siete bateadores y permitió cuatro sencillos.

item.title: [bosoxinjection.com] Cam Schlittler-Dylan Cease Cy Young race has an important Red Sox wrinkle everyone is forgetting
item.dc:creator: Anthony Ranaudo
item.description: The American League East has always been the sport's most star-driven division, even when the standings don't always show it. item.content:encoded:
The American League East has always been the sport's most star-driven division, even when the standings don't always show it. The New York Yankees-Boston Red Sox rivalry alone has produced decades of this, but it's not just those two anymore.
The Toronto Blue Jays have peaked into a real contender, the Tampa Bay Rays are leading this year's race and continue to develop, and the Baltimore Orioles are always one prospect wave away from popping off again. With that much noise in one division, it's easy to lose track of just how much individual talent is walking around it.
Case in point: with Tarik Skubal now pitching for the Los Angeles Dodgers, this year's AL Cy Young race is shaping up to be a battle between two AL East arms, Cam Schlittler and Dylan Cease. That trophy is staying in this division no matter what. But for Red Sox fans, it's worth saying the obvious: if Garrett Crochet had stayed healthy all year, he'd be right in that conversation too, not watching it from the outside looking in.
A healthy Garrett Crochet would've made the 2026 AL Cy Young Award race more interesting
It's easy to forget just how dominant Crochet was in 2025. He went 18-5 with a 2.59 ERA across a league-leading 205.1 innings, struck out a league-best 255 batters, and finished as the AL Cy Young runner-up behind Skubal himself. Take a quick glance at his Baseball Savant page from that season and it reads like a cheat code, elite percentile marks across nearly every meaningful category a pitcher can be graded on. That's the version of Crochet the division rivals were supposed to get again in 2026.
Instead, he was clearly not right from the start, posting an ugly-looking 6.30 ERA across his first six starts before landing on the injured list on April 29 with a shoulder issue that turned into a lat problem after a setback in May. The strikeouts were still there (37 in just 30 innings), but the results were far from pretty, and Boston has been without its ace for basically the entire season since.
Here's where it gets exciting again, though. Crochet threw a bullpen session at Fenway this week, his second since resuming throwing, and interim manager Chad Tracy has been candid that a return this season likely means relief work, not a return to the rotation. Crochet has relief experience already from earlier in his career, and has shown flashes of pure domincance. In 72 bullpen appearances, he logged 73 innings with 85 punchies and 2.71 ERA. In his four postseason relief outings, he has a 0.00 ERA and has struck out 6 of the 14 batters he faced.
He's also made it clear he has zero ego about the role. With Boston fighting to hold onto that second Wild Card spot, a healthy Crochet coming out of the bullpen in high-leverage October moments would be about as fun a development as this fanbase could ask for down the stretch.

item.content:encoded:
Payton Tolle starts with immaculate inning, Roman Anthony gets key hit as Red Sox beat Royals 4-1
The host team defeated the visiting club four to one; the starting pitcher opened the game with an immaculate inning
- 1 minuto de lectura'
BOSTON (AP) — Payton Tolle opened the game with an immaculate inning , Roman Anthony hit a go-ahead single and the Boston Red Sox beat the Kansas City Royals 4-1 on Sunday in a game that’s start was delayed by rain.
Tolle is the first Boston pitcher to throw an immaculate inning (three strikeouts on nine pitches) to start a game since Hall of Famer Pedro Martinez did it on May 18, 2002.
Caleb Durbin hit a solo homer and Trevor Story added a game-breaking two-run single for the Red Sox, who took the final two games of the three-game series.
Carter Jensen drove in the Royals’ run with a pinch-hit single. Kansas City was looking for its first series win in Boston since 2017.
In the seventh, Anthony lined an opposite-field single against reliever Connor Thomas after Craig Kimbrel (1-5) walked the first two batters.
Garrett Whitlock (7-1) was credited with the victory. Aroldis Chapman got the final three outs for his 34th save and the 401st of his career.
Tolle, a hard-throwing 23-year-old left-hander, fanned Nick Loftin called, then got Bobby Witt Jr. and Jac Caglianone swinging in the first.
He went six scoreless innings, striking out seven while allowing four singles.
Noah Cameron gave up a run over six sharp innings.
Durbin belted Cameron’s first pitch into the first row of seats above the Green Monster. Story’s single came off Nate Pearson in the eighth.
Jensen’s RBI single inside the first-base bag tied it.
The club announced Saturday that the finale's start time was pushed back 90 minutes due to the forecast of rain, which came and delayed the first pitch by 1 hour, 50 minutes.
Up next
Royals: RHP Michael Wacha (9-8, 3.25 ERA) is scheduled for the opener of a three-game series in Houston on Tuesday.
Red Sox: LHP Patrick Sandoval (1-5, 4.58) starts Tuesday in the series opener against Texas.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Willson Contreras returns to Red Sox as Anthony Seigler lands on IL - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tim Healey
item.description: Willson Contreras is back with the Red Sox, activated Sunday from the injured list for their finale against the Royals. He collected two hits and a walk in the 4-1 win. The Red Sox didn’t need to think hard about how to open a spot on the active roster: infielder Anthony Seigler went on the injured list with a right wrist issue. “We talked a lot about as guys were getting healthy, the conversation was like, ‘What are you going to do?’” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “Stuff’s going to happen, w
item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras is back with the Red Sox, activated Sunday from the injured list for their finale against the Royals. He collected two hits and a walk in the 4-1 win.
The Red Sox didn’t need to think hard about how to open a spot on the active roster: infielder Anthony Seigler went on the injured list with a right wrist issue.
“We talked a lot about as guys were getting healthy, the conversation was like, ‘What are you going to do?’” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “Stuff’s going to happen, which it always does.”
Contreras missed a dozen games because of a left hamstring strain.
After playing through the leg problem for about a month, Contreras asked the front office to let him more thoroughly rest, figuring a September timeout would serve him well down the stretch and into the playoffs.
On his first day back, he tested it plenty — hustling to first base and advancing to second on an error, moving from first to third on a single.
“I ran a lot today on the field, and my hammy feels pretty good,” Contreras said. “I won’t lie: If I wasn’t feeling really good in [Double-A] Portland, I wasn’t going to play tonight.”
Tracy said: “The point of [going on the IL] was to get [the hamstring] to a point where he felt confident in it, where he can go out and play and not have to worry. And at least like to think we’ve got to that point, which is good.”
In a two-game tuneup with Double-A Portland, Contreras went 2 for 7 with three strikeouts and no walks.
His appearance Saturday yielded a strange episode in the fourth inning. After a ball moved the count to 1-and-1, he called timeout, seemingly to get pine tar. Plate umpire Daniel Bytheway called him back to the plate.
Contreras then all but stopped participating in the plate appearance, leaving the bat on his shoulders for the next four pitches. He struck out looking.
On his way back to the dugout, drawing boos from the Portland crowd, Contreras tossed his bat back toward the plate.
“I didn’t even know until somebody showed it to me this [Sunday] morning,” Tracy said before the game. “I haven’t even seen him and asked him that yet. I think that’s something to do with pine tar.”
Contreras said later Sunday: “I don’t know. You can go ask the umpire. His name is Gary. Thank you.”
The Red Sox didn’t have a diagnosis on Seigler, who hurt himself on a seemingly random swing Saturday, but intended to send him for tests in the coming days.
As the rotation turns
The Red Sox will keep their starting pitchers in line against the Rangers: Patrick Sandoval on Tuesday, Jake Bennett on Wednesday, Sonny Gray on Thursday. Brayan Bello is bumped back to the bullpen following a one-start cameo.
Rehab roundup
The Red Sox will bring Tyron Guerrero (right shoulder inflammation) to Texas and activate him during the Rangers series. They haven’t decided which day. He is eligible to return Wednesday.
Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) told NESN he is planning to return for the Rays series next weekend.
“We’ll call that a goal. It’s not a guarantee,” Tracy said. “It really is dependent on strength numbers in the quad and making sure that’s appropriate, and then he gets through all the sprint volume stuff first, and then we’ll see where he’s at.”
The Sox will leave it up to Rafaela, Tracy added, whether he wants to go on a rehab assignment before returning. Triple-A Worcester is the last affiliate still in season.
Justin Slaten (right elbow inflammation) still has not resumed throwing.
Guest of honor
Beverly native Beckett Connolly, a 10-year-old liver cancer survivor and transplant recipient, threw out a ceremonial first pitch — to hefty applause from the Fenway Park crowd.
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Red Sox's Aroldis Chapman: Shuts door for 34th save
item.dc:creator: RotoWire Staff
item.description: Chapman worked around two walks to earn the save Sunday against the Royals, striking out three in a hitless and scoreless ninth inning. Chapman let the possible tying run get to the plate following a pair of free passes, but he punched out three in a row to hang on for the save. The star southpaw continues to roll, having not blown a save since June 28 against the Yankees. He has a 1.95 ERA, 1.14 WHIP and 68:23 K:BB over 50.2 innings, collecting 34 saves in 36 opportunities.

Chapman let the possible tying run get to the plate following a pair of free passes, but he punched out three in a row to hang on for the save. He has a 1.95 ERA, 1.14 WHIP and 68:23 K:BB over 50.2 innings, collecting 34 saves in 36 opportunities.
